Jazz Picks 
BOA CONSTRICTOR & A \ \ I URAL VINE 
- Vanguard/Apostolic VSD 6511 
A recent deal between Vanguard Records 
and Tenth Street Productions has given rise to 
the new Vanguard/Apostolic label, and this 
LP is one of the first three albums released by 
the fledgling diskery. George Figg.s (vocal & 
guitar) and Ben Syfu ("mostly bass") are 
featured on the set, and they offer a selection 
of folkish, bluesy tunes which are quite ap- 
pealing. More low-keyed than much current 
folk rock product, the tunes on the disk are 
nevertheless distinctive and arresting. This 
package could well aid in getting Vanguard/ 
Apostolic off to a successful start. 
ARS LONGA VITA BREVIS - the Nice - 
Immediate Z 12 52 020 
The Nice, a three-man rock group, has writ- 
ten an extension of the original Allegro from 
Bach's "Brandenburg Concerto No. 3," and 
that composition is Side 2 and the title of this 
album. Classical, rock, and a touch of jazz 
are elements in the piece, and the fusion is 
original and intriguing. Rock -classical inter- 
pretations of "America" from "West Side 
Story" 
and 
Sibelius' 
"Intermezzo 
From 
'Karelia Suite' " are included on Side 
1. 
Many listeners could be attracted to this un- 
usual LP. 
EddieThomas 
Singers 
THE POETRY 
OF MAYA ANGELOU - 
GWP ST 2001 
Black poetess Maya Angelou reads a vari- 
ety of her own work on this, the debut album 
from Gerard W. Purcell's GWP label. The 
artist deals with many subjects, and her 
language 
is 
direct and 
uncompromising. 
Among the poems she reads on the set are 
"Letter To 
An Aspiring Junkie," "White 
Liberals," "To A Man" and "My Life Has 
Turned To Blue." Could gain attention as a 
left -field item. 
THE EDDIE THOMAS SINGERS - Saga/ 
Eros ERO 8049 
The Eddie Thomas Singers render 13 pop 
tunes in smooth, refreshing style. Sparkling 
readings of "Gone With The Wind," "Harlem 
Nocturne," "Moonlight In Vermont," "My 
Funny Valentine," and "I Concentrate On 
You" are featured on the disk. The album is 
most pleasant listening throughout, and there 
could be considerable middle-of-the-road action 
in the offing. 
FURTHER ADVENTURES OF JIMMY & 
WES - Jimmy Smith & Wes Montgomery 
- Verve V6-8766 
The late Wes Montgomery, one of the most 
famed jazz guitarists of all time, and Jimmy 
Smith, the renowned organist, are here show- 
cased in an album that combines their talents 
to the advantage of each. With the exception 
of "Milestones," which uses a horn section, 
all the tunes are performed by Montgomery, 
Smith (on organ) , Grady Tate (on drums) 
and Ray Barretto (on percussion) . An im- 
portant collection. 
EXTRA SOUL PERCEPTION - Monk Higgins 
- Solid State SS 18046 
Monk Higgins' tenor sax is showcased to per- 
fection on a.dozen self -arranged tunes, span- 
ning the spectrum from jazz to soul, and 
touching other musical bases as well. Tunes 
range from straight pop, like "Little Green 
Apples," thru standards, like "Canadian Sun- 
set," to original compositions by Higgins and 
producer Dee Ervin. Higgins is backed by a 
arge group, including strings, and the effect 
will please pop fans, as well as Higgins' 
usual jazz following. 
THE DOUG CARN TRIO 
RING OUT JOY - Ed Summerlin - Avant 
Garde AV 114 
Jazz music has been employed lately in 
church services, and this album of music 
composed, arranged, and conducted by Ed 
Summerlin, is an example of the best of the 
religious jazz works. William Robert Miller 
has written the texts for all the selections, 
and Rosemary Unumaz sings movingly on 
"Gift Of Joy." "The Coming Of Christ" and 
"Liturgy Or The Holy Spirit" are the other 
pieces on the LP. Summerlin has a tenor sax 
solo on "The Coming Of Christ." 
THE DOUG CARN TRIO - Savoy MG 12195 
The Doug Cam Trio (Cam, organ; Gary 
Starling, guitar; and Albert Nicholson, drums) 
offers a slow -cooking, richly simmering set 
of six jazz tunes. (."Free Blues," a swinging, 
full -throttle number, boils right over the pot.) 
Cam's work on "Sometimes I Feel Like A 
Motherless Child" is particularly effective. 
This album should find an enthusiastic recep- 
tion among jazz devotees. 
Classical Picks 
THE HEIFETZ-PIATIGORSKY CON( 
SPOHRJDVORAK- RCA LSC 3068 
Another in the continuing series of record- 
ings spotlighting violinist Jascha Heifetz and 
cellist Gregor Piatigorsky, this album con- 
tains 19th Century German composer Louis 
Spohr's Double String Quartette In D Minor, 
Op. 65 and Anton Dvorak's Piano Trio In E 
Minor, Op. 90 ("Dumky") (Jacob Lateiner is 
the pianist) . As always, Heifetz and Piatigor- 
sky are incomparable, and their latest LP 
will make a fine addition to any classical 
library. 
CLASSIC GUITAR - Julian Bream - RCA 
LSC 3070 
Julian Bream is one of the best classical 
guitarists of our age. and on Side 
1 of this 
album he performs works by two great guitar 
masters of the past, Maurio Giuliani (Grand 
Overture, Op. 
61 and Sonata In C, Op. 15: 
Allegro) and Fernando Sor (Introduction And 
Allegro, Op. 14) 
. Guiliani and Sor were the 
major figures in the guitar's rise to popu- 
larity as a classical instrument in the early 
19th Century. Side 2 of the album carries 
works by Anton Diabelli and Mozart. Excellent 
package.

HANDEL: 
THEODORA - Cardinal 
VSC 
10050/1/2 - ALEXANDER'S 
FEAST 
-e- 
V an gu ard Everyman Classics SRV 282/3 SD 
Vanguard has just brought out two excellent 
Handel choral works that have no other listing 
in the Schwann catalog. "Theodora," an ora- 
torio in 3 acts, is performed by the English 
Chamber Orchestra, Johannes Somary, con- 
ductor, with Heather Harper in the title role, 
on a 3 -record set on the Cardinal label. "Alex- 
ander's Feast," a setting of a poem by John 
Dryden, is performed by the Oriana Concert 
Choir and Orchestra, Alfred Deller, conductor, 
with soloists, on a 2 -record set on the Van- 
guard Everyman Classics label. Both packages 
are musts for Handel lovers. 
AMERICAN 
MUSIC 
FOR 
SYMPHONIC 
WINDS - Eastman Wind Ensemble/Hunsber- 
ger-Decca DL 710163 
The Eastman Wind Ensemble, led by Don- 
ald Hunsberger, offers three pieces by three 
contemporary American composers on this 
album. Masquerade For Band, Op. 102, by 
Vincent Persichetti; Sinfonia No. 4, by Walter 
S. Hartley; and Sinfonietta For Concert Band, 
by Ingolf Dahl are all of interest and are 
very well performed by the Eastman Ensem- 
ble. This LP merits attention.

ChiCoin Bows `Champagne' 6-P 
Features 'Swivel Score Rack' 
CHICAGO - Chicago Coin released 
their 
latest 
bowler, 
the 
6 -player 
"Champagne" to the trade last week. 
Operators will be pleased with the 
Chicoin exclusive 'swivel score rack' 
which allows easy access - front or 
back - for maintenance. 
Champagne, features the popular 
regulation with 'Beer Frame' feature, 
which lights up during the fifth frame 
of the game. Other ways to play are: 
flash-o-matic, Red Pin, Step-up and 
Dual Flash. 
At left is ChiCoin's 
latest bowler, 'Cham- 
pagne', a six -player 
with regulation 'Beer 
Frame' feature. 
The new bowler also features .15' 
play or 2 for .25e, but is adjustable to 
10' and 25' play. It also has individual 
coin chutes - 5e, 10' and 25`. 
Champagne is housed in a modern 
styled cabinet with a wide playfield, 
and comes in 
161/2 and 131 feet 
lengths. Additional 4' and 8' sections 
are available. 
The Chicago Coin nationwide net- 
work of distributors are now preview- 
ing Champagne in their showrooms. 
For details see the distributor in your 
area. 
ICMOA FACED WITH 
NEW ANTI-PINGAME 
LEGISLATION IN ILL. 
CHICAGO - Fred Gain, executive 
secretary of the Illinois Coin Machine 
Operators Association, reported late 
last week that Senator Harris 
W. 
Sewell of Dupage County introduced 
to the Illinois Senate on Tuesday, 
March 18th, a bill (Senate Bill 0592) 
that, if passed, would make it, "unlaw- 
ful to keep or use a pinball game in 
the state of Illinois and provide for 
seizure and destruction of said games." 
Gain said, "there are four parts to 
this bill which would affect our op- 
erators. Copies of the bill have not 
been released as yet, they should be 
in my hands within the next few days 
and I can assure you we will fight 
this latest legislative move with every 
ounce of strength in 
our bodies. 
BALLY RINGS BELL 
WITH INITIAL 
STOCK OFFERING 
NEW YORK - Last March 17, 1968, 
Bally Mfg. Corp., registered an initial 
common stock offer of 275,000 shares 
($4,675,000) with the Securities and 
Exchange Commission. 
After approximately one year, last 
week the stock was placed on the mar- 
ket. It was quickly oversubscribed 
and bid to a premium above its $15 -a - 
share offering price. Shortly there- 
after, some dealers were quoting the 
shares at around $22 bid, $23 asked. 
Underwriters 
led 
by 
Saunders, 
Stivers & Co., and Coenen & Co., 
made the offering.

SCHNELLER 
REVEALS 
PLANS 
FOR NAT'L. 8 -BALL TOURNEY 
AT NYSOG MEET - LATE 70's 
Jack Wilson presided at the March 
19th New York State Operators Guild 
meeting, 
at 
which 
Len 
Schneller 
dropped the bomb shell when he told 
the assembled members that 
U.S. 
Billiards president Albert Simon and 
himself have been planning towards 
the staging of a national 8 -ball tourna- 
ment to take place in the late 1970's. 
According to Schneller's plans the 
four division winners of 128 regional 
tourneys will be flown to an undeter- 
mined city for the grand champion- 
ship. He further revealed that nearly 
one -quarter million dollars would be 
collected thru the coin boxes at local 
tourneys for the most magnificent 
series of prizes ever offered in a tour- 
ney of this nature. 
Schneller was at the meeting 
to 
participate in a discussion on the 
Guild -sponsored 8 -ball tourney which 
just recently concluded. He learned 
that members were anxious to begin 
their second tourney in late August. 
Further details on this development 
will appear in the next issue of Cash 
Box. 
SUGERMAN SHIPS WORLD'S 
NEW YORK - The El Dorado, world's 
largest and most ornate carousel, once 
the showpiece of Steeplechase Park in 
Coney Island, Brooklyn, left the U.S. 
aboard the Japan freighter Kohoh 
Maur for Japan last Friday, March 
21st. 
Myron Sugerman International got 
the assignment from a Japanese firm 
to locate and purchase the finest and 
greatest carousel in the world for 
the Toshimaen Amusement Park in 
Tokyo. 
Remembering the Carousel, which 
had been in Steeplechase since 1911 
but moved to a storage house in Wild - 
LARGEST CAROUSEL 
wood, NJ by owner Alan Hawes when 
the park closed in 1965, Sugerman 
located it and purchased it for his 
client. 
The carousel was loaded into six 
ship containers at pier #8 under the 
personal supervision of Hans Vanden- 
Dorp, a Sugerman representative. 
Sugerman commented, "the carousel 
will be missed by those whose memo- 
ries of Coney Island are awakened by 
the sound of the great organ the smell 
of popcorn and hotdogs and the salty 
breezes of the sea 
. 
. 
. while the 
children of Japan welcome the world's 
greatest merry-go-round."

Rock-Ola Stages, In Factory, Phono - Vending Training 
Shown above is Rock-Ola's Warren Wheatman, the firm's sound technician and Edward Lorkowski, the field service 
engineer for vending; as they explain carious details of Rock-Ola's phonographs and vending equipment to servicemen. 
CHICAGO - Rock -Ola Mfg. Corp. 
played host to a group of music and 
vending service technicians from var- 
ious parts of the United States for five 
days çMarch 10-14) during which an 
extensive series of service sessions 
were held right in the factory. The 
school, which began Monday morn- 
ing and ended the following Friday 
afternoon, covered all phases of the 
Rock -Ola products in the vending and 
music equipment lines, both electrical 
and mechanical. 
62 
William Findlay, Rock-Ola's Field 
Service Engineer for phonographs. 
was the main instructor. Electrical 
and sound instruction on the phono- 
graph 
was conducted 
by 
Warren 
Wheatman, Rock-Ola's sound techni- 
cian, while the vending line was taught 
by 
Edward 
Lorkowski, 
Rock-Ola's 
Field Service Engineer for Vending. 
The visiting service men learned the 
operation of the Rock -Ola phonograph 
"from the ground up" b 
actually 
assembling a phonograph from all of 
its components. 
The service men in attendance were: 
Bernard Thompson, Syracuse, New 
York: 
Louis Avoglia, North Bergen. 
New Jersey: Charles Beam, Manhat- 
tan, Kansas; Robert Greatens, Green 
Bay, Wisconsin: Richard Allen, Apple- 
ton. Wisconsin: Lyle Olson, Marinette, 
Wisconsin: Dale Johnson, Menominee, 
Michigan; Earl Hoot and Pete Falco, 
Houston, Texas: Paul Vidmar, Den- 
ver, Colorado. 
turers, and operators all get together 
and make these places what they should 
be "family amusement centers" with 
no pornographic pictures, movie ma- 
chines, or anything that may destroy 
the image of good clean amusement.' 
Let no one infer from this statement 
that 
I am opposed to panorams, movie 
machines or any kind of coin operated 
audio, visual machine for arcades. This 
is not true. Anyone of these machines is 
welcome equipment in an arcade where 
families and youngsters are the principal 
patrons, provided the films are clean 
and wholesome. 
I do not believe that "girlie" or porno- 
graphic films should be shown in such 
arcades. Not necessarily do these films 
corrupt anyone but because 
it is bad 
public relations, and destroys the image 
of the arcade which is allegedly offering 
clean amusement. In arcades for adults 
only anything that the law allows can be 
shown. 
This writer is a firm believer in not 
exposing youngsters to some of the bad 
habits and escape 
pleasures that we 
foolish elders indulge in; namely, petty 
gambling, cigarettes, alcohol and porno- 
graphy. 
Maybe this writer is old fashioned, but 
perhaps what is wrong with the youth 
of today is that they are exposed to such 
literature as "Candy", "Fanny Hill", "Lady 
Chatterly", 
rather than "Tom 
Swift', 
Frank Meriwell" and "Horatio Alger". 
Our own arcades have plenty of movie 
machines and panorams, but because 
youngsters are the principal patrons of 
these places, we show only football films, 
cartoons, old news reels, scenes from old 
silent movies and many other films that 
youngsters like and enjoy.

Dubois To Blue Note 
As Nat'l Promo Mgr. 
NEW 
YORK - Duke Dubois has 
joined the Blue Note/Solid State divi- 
sion of Liberty/UA in the post of na- 
tional promotion manager, reporting 
to the label's general manager, Mel 
Fuhrman. 
Dubois moves to the label from his 
post as promotion manager for New 
York's Metro Distributors. He entered 
the business as a salesman for Cam- 
bridge Distributors, and moved on to 
assignments in sales and promotion 
for Big Town and, subsequently Por- 
ter Distributors. Expanding his expe- 
rience from the distributor to the 
manufacturer level, 
Dubois joined 
ABC Records as a promotional field 
representative for two years, before 
joining Metro. 
Dubois (I.) & Fuhrman 
The evening concert will feature Dai u 
Brubeck and Gerry Mulligan, Woody 
Herman Orchestra, Sly and the Fam- 
ily Stone, O.C. Smith, and the World's 
Greatest Jazz Band. 
A solo concert by James Brown 
will be presented Sunday afternoon. 
The festival will close Sunday evening 
with the "Schlitz Mixed Bag," spon- 
sored by the Jos. Schlitz Brewing Co. 
and featuring Herbie Hancock, S.B. 
King, Buddy Rich Orchestra, Buddy 
Tate, Joe Turner, Winter featuring 
.Johnny Winter, and Led Zeppelin. 
Festival producer George Wein stat- 
ed that he expects this to be the big- 
gest and most exciting festival in the 
history of Newport events. 
Ives Music Firm 
Reorganization 
NEW YORK - There's been a re- 
organization of Wayfarer Music, the 
Burl Ives music publishing unit, ac- 
cording to Helen Payne, vp and gen- 
eral manager. 
In line with this re -organization, 
Wayfarer will make available for the 
first time for outside recordings, the 
complete Burl Ives' catalogs of orig- 
inal compositions by Ives and other 
writers. This material has never been 
offered before and encompasses over 
500 original copyrights 
in the folk, 
country & western, Christmas, kiddie, 
and contemporary markets. 
All material is available through 
Wayfarer Music, 140 W. 57th St., New 
York. 
Lou Stein Returns 
NEW YORK - Pianist Lou Stein has 
cut a disk for Murbo Records. Jimmy 
Krondes, Murbo head, co -produced the 
date with Stein, who opens here this 
week for a 1 -month engagement at the 
Downbeat. Topside of the single is 
"That Old Time Flavor."

THE WINTER CONSORT - A&M SP 4170 
The Winter Consort, headed by Paul Winter, 
who plays saxophone on this album, performs 
a variety of pieces from different periods 
of music. The musicians of the Winter Consort 
display their versatility in numbers by Jobim, 
Villa-Lobos, Joni 
Mitchell, and 
Dowland, 
among others, and the result is an interest-_ 
ing and often arresting LP. Listeners who 
enjoy experimentation in music will want 
to add this recording to their collections. 
CLEANLINESS AND GODLINESS SNIFFLE 
BAND'S GREATEST HITS - Vanguard VSD 
79285 
Performing with tongues firmly in cheek, 
the Cleanliness and Godliness Skiffle Band 
serves up twelve plunkety-plunk ditties in a 
style calculated to provide the listener with 
hearty chuckles galore. The group uses man- 
dolins, wood blocks, and harmonica as well 
as serious instruments and vocals to create 
an album filled with cheerful lunacy. Stan- 
dards and original tunes penned by members 
of the act are given the full zany treatment. 
A most disarming LP. 
MARIACHI DE HERIBERTO ACEVES - 
ENCANTADO VOL. II - UA Latino L 31039/ 
LS 61039 
This is Heriberto Aceves' second album 
to be distributed in the U.S., and it is 
a 
most happy event. Aceves has chosen ten 
traditional Mexican tunes, and with his fine' 
band, creates a delightful LP of Mariachi 
music. Lilting, buoyant, melodic sounds offer 
the listener an enchanting musical experience 
The set should be popular in Latin markets, 
and could find favor in good music areas in 
general.

VIVALDI, TARTINI, PURCELL, ZANETTI - 
Camerata Bariloche - Odyssey 32 16 0310 
The Camerata Bariloche, an Argentinian 
Baroque chamber emsemble, makes a very 
impressive U.S. recording debut with this 
LP. Led by Alberto Lysy, violinist and con- 
ductor, the aggregation performs works by

bers of the Camerata Bariloche should build 
up a dedicated American following if they 
continue to make albums like this. 
BARTOK/DOHNANYI/KODALY FOR VIOLIN 
AND PIANO - Gerle/Benoit-Westminster WST 
17150 
The spirit of Hungarian folk music dominates 
this album of works by Bela Bartok, Ernst 
Von Dohnanyi and Zoltan Kodaly. Violinist 
Robert Gerle, who performs on the album with 
Regis Benoit accompanying on piano, points 
out that "A characteristic of folk music is that 
the tune is not intended for, or limited to, 
one particular instrument or group of in- 
struments," and all the pieces on this set 
exist in some other form. In their form here, 
they are most engaging and are engagingly 
rendered by Gerle and Benoit.

BETHESDA, 
MARYLAND - John 
(Red) Wallace, prominent West Vir- 
ginia operator -distributor and former 
MOA 
president, 
died last 
Sunday 
March 30th at the National Institute 
of Health here in Bethesda. Mr. Wal- 
lace was recuperating from serious 
surgery 
which 
was 
performed 
on 
March 14th in an attempt to check 
what was termed "a terminal illness", 
when he passed away. 
Funeral services were held Wed- 
nesday April 2nd at the Tyree Funeral 
Home in Oak Hill, W. Va., Mr. Walla- 
ce's home town and seat of his distri- 
buting organization Wallace & Wallace 
Dist. MOA president Howard Ellis and 
executive vice president Fred Granger 
attended the services, as did George 
Hincker of Rock -Ola Mfg. Corp. whose 
products Wallace & Wallace Dist. han- 
dled. Other familiar industry person- 
nel, many local tradesmen and other 
long time friends were also in atten- 
dance. 
Immediate survivors include his wife 
Jean, their twins John, Jr. and Debbie 
and his brother and partner Eugene. 
Cards and letters may be mailed to 
Wallace &Wallace, 401 Jones Avenue, 
Oak Hill, W. Va. 25901.

Fine example of industry public relations on the move is the familiar Holmark 
Coin Equipment, Ltd. truck which regularly shoots around the wide central area 
of Great Britain servicing their hundreds of amusement machine locations. 
Actually, vehicle shown above is only one of vast service fleet operated by the 
Morecambe, England based games operation. Tradesmen will notice, as do 
thousands of British citizens, the Bally Manufacturing Corp. insignia prominent- 
ly displayed on the hood as well as on other spots on the van. Holmark's slogan 
"from coast to coast your amusement host" refers to the firm's territorial con- 
centration which stretches between the Irish and North Seas.

Jim Ladwig Joins 
Album Graphics 
CHICAGO - Album Graphics has an- 
nounced the appointment of Jim Lad - 
wig to its staff. For the past eight 
years, Ladwig has been art and ad 
director of Mercury Records. 
Album Graphics was formed 
to 
"solve creative packaging problems 
and to produce unusual and specialty 
albums for manufacturers at compet- 
itive prices." 
The east coast affiliate of AG is 
Craig Braun, which specializes in the 
design and printing of promotional 
materials for .the record industry. 
Braun claims pioneering efforts in the 
popular usage of self-adhesive labels 
as a merchandising aid for album 
and tape cartridge product. The com- 
pany is headquartered in New York, 
with plants in New Jersey and Chicago. 
AGI developed from the wide album 
manufacturing experience of Donald 
W. Kosterka, who has produced such 
packaging as the Connoisseur Collec- 
tion's Singing Nun and Missa Luba, 
, 
and Limelight albums with pop -out 
folds. 
AGI produced the Four Seasons 
Gold Edition which utilized gold foil I 
laminated board and was embossed 
and die cut into a two -record album. 
Company has also done three albums 
for Spanky and our Gang and Paul 
Mauriat. 
AGI has facilities for complete di- 
rect mail services in addition to its 
album production facilities for em- 
bossing, printing on board, foil, octag- 
onal shapes, movable parts, posters, 
inside leaflets, tape boxes, and other 
collateral material. 
Ladwig, 
who 
presently 
lives 
in 
Evanston, Illinois, attended the Art 
Institute of Chicago, Bradley Univer- 
sity and the American Academy of 
Art. During his eight years with Mer- 
cury, he won numerous awards, in- 
cluding the Art Directors Club of New 
York and Chicago, the Society of Ty- 
pographic Arts and the Chicago So- 
ciety of Communication Arts. In 1968 
he was awarded the first annual Roll- 
ing Stone Award for Excellence in 
Advertising, and he has been a nom- 
inee for Best Album Cover from the 
National Academy of Recording Arts 
and Sciences.

Multi -Lingual La Manchas From MCA 
NEW YORK - The "Man of La Man- 
cha" returns home in a figurative 
sense next month when the Spanish 
language original cast album is re- 
leased on the MCA label throughout 
Latin America and on Decca Records 
in the United States. The Latin the- 
atre goers have seen the hit in Mexico 
City and Buenos Aires. 
The original cast album was re- 
corded by the MCA Records Interna- 
tional affiliate in Mexico, Orfeon-Vid- 
eovox, -under - the 'personal supervi- 
sion of Mariano Rivera Conde. 
The album- which will be rush re- 
leased in the United States, marks the 
third original cast version available in 
this country on one of the MCA labels. 
The Broadway original cast album 
was on MCA's Kapp label and has 
been a consistent best-seller since its 
release. In 1968, Decca recorded the 
original London cast album, complete 
with dialog and music and this has 
also achieved "excellent" sales in 
the United States and the English 
speaking markets of the world, the 
label reports. 
In addition to the forthcoming Span- 
ish cast version, MCA Records Inter- 
national VP Dick Broderick announced 
that plans are being finalized to re- 
lease in the U.S. the French "Man Of 
La Mancha" with the Paris original 
cast starring, Jacques_ Brel and Amer -

NEW YORK - Based on heavy ad-

with Dylan on "Girl Of The North 
Country."

Bell's `1st Stage' 
Spring LP Release 
NEW YORK - Three new LP's com- 
prise the 'first stage' of Bell Records 
Spring album release, according to 
Iry Biegel, vice president and direc- 
tor of sales for the label. 
Heading off the release is "Dial -A - 
Hit," an all-star package of stone 
smashes performed by the Box Tops, 
the Delfonics, Bobby Russell, the Mas- 
queraders, James & Bobby Purify, Al 
Greene, the O'Jays and Merrilee Tush. 
Also in the release is "Counter- 
point," the new Chad Mitchell al- 
bum, titled after his successful one- 
man show, and "Legend," debut LP 
of the British underground group of 
the same name. The Legend set is the 
first "return ticket" of Bell's "trans - 
Atlantic traffic" of local European 
talent, produced by Sandy Roberton 
for English and Continental release on 
the British Bell logo. 
Biegel said the `second stage' of 
Bell's Spring release involves 'special 
project' albums, with separate an- 
nouncements to be made shortly.

London To Distrib 
Goland's New Age 
NEW YORK - London Records has 
just completed arranjements to han- 
dle national distribution for New Age 
Records, a label recently formed by 
Arnold Goland. The deal incorporates 
worldwide distribution through Lon- 
don's parent firm Decca Record Co. 
Ltd., of Great Britain. 
Walt Maguire, national singles sales 
& A&R chief for London, noted that 
the first product from New Age will 
be made available this week. Premiere 
side is "Come With Me" by the Fringe 
Benefit, featuring a chamber music 
theme 
from Bach's 
"Brandenburg 
Concerto #6" with vocal and counter - 
melody. An LP is planned by this 
group and other singles will be re- 
leased shortly from several acts sign- 
ed to New Age. 
Goland started his musical involve- 
ment while at Cornell University and 
gained a reputation through work in 
producing, arranging and composing. 
He was most recently associated with 
Jack Gold, A&R head at Columbia, as 
arranger and producer and wrote "It 
Hurts To Say Goodbye" with Gold. 
The song has just been released here 
after reaching international promi- 
nence as a European hit.

Box - April 19, 1969 
NASHVILLE SKYLINE - Bob Dylan - Co- 
lumbia KCS 9825 
When we first put this album on the turn- 
table, we didn't recognize the voice that 
came out of the speaker. We figured it must 
be Bob Dylan, and it was. He's changed the 
quality of his voice 
(he's trying 
to sing 
more) . The set has Nashville backing and 
features Johnny Cash on one track, "Girl 
From The North Country," and it is almost, 
though not quite, a country record. It's not 
a country record, because it's Dylan, and Dy- 
lan, no matter what his influences, is never 
quite anything but himself. 
1776 - Original Cast - BOS 3310 
This humanizing musical tribute 
to the 
Founding Fathers has garnered the uncom- 
promising praise of most of the critics. In 
the cast LP, the Sherman Edwards music 
and lyrics must stand alone. As an intergra- 
ted score, it leaves nothing to be desired in 
appropriateness and in suggesting the musi- 
cal flavor of the Revolutionary time. Yet, 
there isn't much to carry away from the 
plotline nor true melodic freshness - except, 
perhaps, the haunting anti -war song, "Momma 
Look Sharp." The production on records is 
very much alive. This is a smash show and 
its cast LP counterpart is a must for the 
theatre shelf. 
THE PROGRESSIVE BLUES EXPERIMENT 
- Johnny Winter - Imperial LP 12431 
The current bonanza of interest in white 
blues belter Johnny Winter is responsible for 
the release of this album of old cuts. Winter 
is now signed 
to Columbia, but his first 
charted effort is this set, which showcases 
him in 
a host of energetic blues tracks 
(some of them self -penned) recorded, accord- 
ing to the album jacket, at the Vulcan Gas 
Company in Austin, Texas. On the charts 
now, "The Progressive Blues Experiment" 
stands a good chance to become a major 
hit. 
ELVIS SINGS FLAMING STAR - Elvis 
Presley - RCA Camden CAS 2304 
This album of old Elvis Presley cuts on 
RCA's budget label, Camden, has hit the 
charts, a fact that attests to the continuing 
high level of popularity that Elvis still en- 
joys. In addition to the title tune, which is 
from an old western of the same name in 
which Elvis starred, the set contains "Too 
Much Monkey 
Business," 
"Yellow 
Rose 
Of Texas," "Do The Vega," "Tiger Man" 
and five others. A package to stock. 
NANCY - Nancy Sinatra - Reprise RS 6333 
Nancy Sinatra 
should garner numerous 
spins and sales with her latest album. The 
lark's sultry voice has gained her a big fol- 
lowing, which should be pleased with the 
set. Her new single, "God Knows I Love 
You," which was recently on the charts, leads 
off the LP and is followed by eleven others, in- 
cluding 
"Big 
Boss 
Man," 
"Son -Of -A - 
Preacher Man" 
and "For Once 
In My 
Life." Package should be showing 
action 
soon. 
SONGS FROM A ROOM - Leonard,Cohen - 
Columbia CS 9767 
As expected, Leonard Cohen's second album 
is already making a dent in the charts, and 
should prove a strong seller for him. Imagery 
is Cohen's forte, and there is plenty of imagery 
here for his loyal following to sink their 
teeth into. With one exception ("The Parti- 
san") , all the tunes are Cohen originals, de- 
livered in his familiar low-keyed style. "A 
Bunch Of Lonesome Heros," "Seems So Long 
Ago, Honey" and "Tonight Will Be Fine" 
are a few of the sides.

LORD - Northern California State Youth 
Choir/Edwin R. Hawkins - Century 31016 
The Northern California State Youth Choir, 
lead by Edwin R. Hawkins, has come up 
with what may well become, because of its 
unique spontaneous and universally appeal - 
ling quality, the first huge hit gospel album. 
The single, "Oh Happy Day, 
from the LP,. 
has already begin to break big all over the 
country. Buddah has acquired the national 
sales rights to the single and album and will 
soon release them on the Pavilion label. The 
Choir, organized by Hawkins and Betty Wat- 
son, has to be heard to be believed. Watch 
this set very, very carefully. 
TALES TO WARM YOUR MIND - Irish 
Rovers - Decca DL 75081 
The zestful harmony and humor of the 
Irish Rovers has established the group as a 
strong in -person and disk attraction, and 
this collection of folk tales, both old and 
new, should be another strong outing. The 
group's recent noisemaking "Lily The Pink" 
leads off an entertaining batch of songs which 
also includes "The Village Of Brambleshire 
Wood," "Mrs. Crandall's Boardinghouse" and 
"Minstrel Of Cranberry Lane." 
IT'S OUR THING - Isley Brothers -T -Neck 
TNS 3001 
The Isley Brothers' Top 5 "It's Your Thing" 
disk brought the trio back on the record scene 
with a bang, and their follow-up album (the 
best Isley set yet) should keep them hot. Many 
of the tunes here stem from ideas and lines 
in "It's Your Thing," and the set has unusual 
unity. "I Know Who You've Been Socking 
It To," "I Must Be Losing My Touch" and 
"Give The Women What They Want" are 
first -draw. Album should be in for progres- 
sive rock as well as R&B play.

and humor

Beatles Counter ATV's Northern Bid 
LONDON - The Beatles have coun- 
tered Associated TeleVision's bid for 
Northern Songs with one of their own. 
It is worth £2,400,000, and represents 
an offer of 42 shillings and sixpence 
per two shilling share. The ATV bid, 
comprising shares, loan stock and 
cash, is worth just under 37 shillings 
and eightpence. 
The Beatle strategy is to acquire a 
minimum of 983,501 shares to add to 
their present holding of 1,516,000 with a 
maximum ceiling of 
1 million. Their 
merchant banker, Henry Ansbacher, is 
contributing 
£11/4 
million 
to 
their 
£2,400,000 bid. 
In effect, The Beatles are offering to 
buy approximately 
four 
in 
every 
seven shares held in Northern Songs 
by uncommitted holders, with the re- 
maining three to be retained by the 
holder. 
Sir Lew's Reaction 
ATV chief Sir Lew Grade described 
the Beatle bid as "deceptive," and 
thought that "intelligent shareholders" 
will accept the ATV offer, which 
would give equity interest in "a first- 
class and growing organization with 
a proven management." 
The Beatles are open in their dislike 
of ATV's plan to capture Northern 
Songs. They have intimated that if the 
ATV bid is successful, they will not be 
happy "to continue, let alone renew 
their existing contracts with Northern 
Songs" which are valid until 1973. 
That is clear notice to ATV, at pres- 
ent controlling 35% of the company. 
that if it secures Northern Songs, it 
can expect only the required minimum 
of 24 songs from The Beatles over 
the next four years. 
John Lennon and Paul McCartney 
are wooing shareholders by saying 
that if their counter bid succeeds, 
Northern Songs will get first refusal 
on their songwriting services for a 
further two years. In addition, George 
Harrison, with 24 copyrights to his 
credit, would sign with the company, 
and so would Ringo Starr, who has 
just begun composing efforts. 
A further carrot dangled is "the 
feasibility 
of offering 
to Northern 
Songs certain of their other entertain- 
ment interests." If The Beatles tri- 
umph, they will strengthen the North- 
ern Songs board with some financial 
specialists and "an expert in music 
publishing." 
This latter intention underlines the 
total rift now existing between The 
Beatles 
and Northern's 
managing 
director Dick James, who has headed 
the company since its inception in 
1962. James has a management agree- 
ment that expires like the Lennon and 
McCartney contracts in 1973. 
If successful, the Beatle offer will 
give them a holding of just over 50% 
in Northern Songs. It may be ques- 
tioned by the official takeover panel, 
which normally disapproves of partial 
bids. 
Triumph's Role 
5% of the Northern Songs equity is 
held by Triumph Investment Trust, 
which controls 90% of Nemperor Hold- 
ings, the company founded by the late 
Brian Epstein. The atmosphere be- 
tween Triumph and The Beatles is 
less than cordial following Triumph's 
recent unsuccessful High Court move 
to establish that an estimated £1 mil- 
lion in Beatle royalties should be paid 
by EMI to Nemperor and not to The 
Beatles' Apple company. EMI declared 
in court that it will not pay the royal- 
ties to any party until the dispute is 
resolved. 
Triumph chief Tom Whyte described 
The Beatles' intention to contest ATV's 
offer for Northern Songs as "topsy 
turvy" and "illogical." Initial stock 
market reaction to the counter bid was 
disappointment at 
its 
terms, 
and 
Northern's share value 
dipped as 
speculators pulled out.

Edel Offers Ad -Music Industries Link 
NEW YORK - Advertising has ad- 
vanced its musical outlook so rapidly 
during the past few years that agency 
work along Madison Ave. for artists, 
arrangers, composers and producers 
has become a major area for both ex- 
pansion and experiment. Realizing 
that there are very few channels be- 
tween agencies and music figures, Her- 
man Edel Associates has instituted a 
series of moves to essentially improve 
relations linking the record and ad- 
vertising fields. 
As a two-way communicator, Edel's 
firm has lined up an impressive roster 
of artists, writers and producers to 
offer talent to ad clients through its 
representatives. And, the company is 
readily available as a musical con - 
DOING THEIR OWN THING FOR 
TRO are Hal Hester (3rd from left) 
and Danny Apolinar (to Hester's left), 
composers of the score of "Your Own 
Thing," the hit off-Broadway musical 
which recently won a New York Drama 
Critics Circle award as Best Musical 
of 
1968. Hester and Apolinar have 
signed an exclusive writing pact with 
The Richmond Organization. Shown at 
the signing ceremonie at TRO's Co- 
lumbus Circle headqulters with the 
composers are (I. to r.) Minton Fran- 
cis (standing) , TRO vice president and 
executive directors; Marvin Cane, TRO 
vice president, 
who conducted the 
negotiations which led to the signing 
of the pair; David Platz, TRO inter- 
national director; and Al Brackman, 
executive vice president and general 
manager of TRO. Initial project in the 
Hester-Apolinar-TRO contract is the 
David Black production of "Alice," an 
adaptation of the Lewis Carroll stories, 
"Alice In Wonderland" and "Alice 
Through The Looking Glass." Book of 
"Alice ' is by N. Richard Nash. The 
show is currently set for production 
on Broadway next autumn. 
sultant to advertising planners seeking 
suggested approaches or personnel 
capable of creating or performing ma- 
terial of a required sort. 
The company's credits span rock 
with Neil Diamond's current Buick ad 
to classical with Carlos Montoya per- 
forming for a Gulf commercial. Touch- 
ing most of the areas in between these 
extremes, 
Herbie 
Hancock's 
jazz 
work, Walter Raim's MOR style, Jake 
Holmes' folk, Scharf & Dorough ("Give 
a Damn") , and more show the scope 
of artists whose material for commer- 
cials is handled exclusively through 
Edel Assoc. On the other hand, lesser 
known 
behind -the -scenes 
figures 
through Edel have come up with a 
series of other 
well-known though 
usually un -name -associated spots in- 
cluding the "Wear Your Love Like 
Heaven" adaptation of Donovan's hit 
for Love Cosmetics and the Virginia 
Slims theme "You've Come a Long

the new Chantilly ads. 
In addition to the work aspects, Edel 
has avoided turning all the music men 
into one -minute -songsters by generally 
producing a full-length session for 
each original theme and trimming 
from the complete track to reduce the 
time for commercial use. 
Ella Logan Dies 
Of Cancer At 56 
BURLINGAME, CALIF. - Ella Logan, 
who starred on radio with Al Jolson 
and Rudy Valee and originally played 
Shara in "Finian's Rainbow," died 
last week (1) at Peninsula Hospital. 
The 56 -year -old artist had been hos- 
pitalized for a week before dying of 
cancer. 
Born in Glasgow, Miss Logan made 
her first stage appearance at the age 
of 3, and played Europe before coming 
to America at 18. She debuted here in 
"Calling All Stars" and performed 
also in "George White's Scandals," 
"Sons of Fun," "Show Time" and her 
starring role in "Finian's Rainbow" 
on Broadway. She also did various 
nightclub shows and appeared in sev- 
eral films, including 
"Top 
of the 
Town," "Flying Hostess" and "Wom- 
an Chases Man." 
In recent years Miss Logan had done 
spots on various television shows, the 
last being Mery Griffin's "St. Patrick's 
Day" special. 
She is survived by a brother, Jim 
Logan; and a sister, Mrs. Ann Arthur. 
She is to be buried this week (5) at 
Holy Cross Cemetery in West Los An- 
geles.

New Budd To Blossom 
With MGM LP Release 
NEW YORK - .Julie Budd's recent 
appearance on the Ed Sullivan Show 
might not have seemed far removed 
from her earlier tv appearances, but 
with the release of her second MGM 
album this week, the youngster's ca- 
reer takes a less subtle change. The 
new album concentrates on her capa- 
bilities as an artist for the young 
adult and soft -sound audiences that 
have reacted strongly to her televi- 
sion appearances. 
According to 
her producer 
and 
manager Herb Bernstein, Julie Budd's 
first LP sought to establish her as 
a hit artist by presenting material 
with singles potential (most notably 
the "All's Quiet on West 23rd" noise- 
maker) . From the response of people 
who were upset that the Budd on rec- 
ord was not the Budd from tv, Bern- 
stein, his artist and MGM decided 
to begin development of Julie's talent 
in the new vein. 
Strong use of standards, 
with 
a 
good deal of contemporary material; 
pop arrangements with a young fresh- 
ness; and generally working almost 
in nightclub act fashion will better 
define the Budd-ing talent on the new 
set. 
She is also embarking on a greater 
schedule of personal appearances in 
support of the LP, including a string 
of Mery Griffin Show spots (which 
began last week and will continue for 
the next five Fridays), two upcoming 
Sullivan dates signed immediately 
after her last performance on the 
network program; 
a Mike Douglas 
spot; and a number of live shows 
to offer her new club act. 
Junior Streisand 
Miss Budd was also selected by 
the planning committee of a Barbra 
Streisand celebration at the Friar's 
Club 
in 
New 
York 
next 
week 
to appear as a parody/imitation of 
the guest of honor. Julie has been 
compared to Streisand in her tv pre- 
sentations, which mildly upset Bern- 
stein since he has been working at 
developing his artist as an individual 
talent in her own right. However, he 
noted, at least .she is being held up 
for comparison to one of the best. 
Besides, he added, Julie is just about 
to turn fifteen, and most people re- 
alize that she is still developing into 
her own kind of artist. 
Although Bernstein has trimmed 
his own activities to devote major 
attention to the new Julie Budd, now 
that her activities have picked up 
momentum, he has had time to step 
up efforts for his recently released 
Metromedia album "Herb Goldstein's 
New Crusade." He is also currently 
working with composer/singer Tony 
Wine who is soon to record her first 
sides for RCA; and planning exten- 
sion of his publishing and production 
operations in a move soon to be com- 
pleted.

MERCY - Ohio Express - Buddah BDS5037 
The Ohio Express is still going strong on the 
right hit track, with the title tune of their 
latest album being their current chart rider, 
and their usual collection of bubble gum fans 
will want to own this set. The group's last hit, 
"Sweeter Than Sugar," is also present, as are 
several new tunes in the same vein, including 
Gimme, Gimme," "Come On Down Mary - 
dun" and "Nighttime." 
PLAYGIRL - Thee Prophets - Kapp KS 3596 
The rock sound of the mid -West has a light 
and lyrical quality all its own and Thee Proph- 
ets, just coming off the charts with the title 
tune of this album, are top exponents of that 
sound. In addition to the Top 40 "Playgirl" 
deck, the group's new single, "Some Kind Of 
Wonderful," will also provide a spark. "Man 
Enough," "Heartbreak Avenue" and "Kind Of 
A Drag" will provide some solid program- 
ming. 
LISTEN TO THE MOVIES WITH FERRANTE 
& TEICHER - United Artists UAS 6701 
Pianists Ferrante & Teicher serve up a batch 
of title tunes from current and recent flicks on 
their latest LP, and the result is a package 
that's bound to appeal to the duo's following. 
Among the numbers on the set are "Chitty 
Chitty Bang Bang," "Funny Girl," "Oliver" 
and "Yellow Submarine." F & T can always be 
counted on to pull in good sales, and their new 
album should continue their pattern of 
success. 
VINTAGE ROCK - Bill Deal & Rhondels - 
Heritage HTS 35,003 
Two chart hits, the recent "May I" and the 
current "I've Been Hurt" should open the 
sales door wide for this debut album by Bill 
Deal and the Rhondels. The set mixes current 
hits with sonne newer material and deserves a 
lot of play on outlets featuring a soft -rock 
sound. "Touch Me," "Hooked On A Feeling," 
"Hey Bulldog," "Soulful Strut" and "I'm 
Gonna Make You Love Me" will help sell the 
set.

LETTERS TO A BLACK BOY - Bob Teague 
- Bell 6029 
NBC-TV newscaster Bob Teague has a best- 
selling book with "Letters To A Black Boy," 
and this album, which consists of readings 
from the book, together with songs and music 
composed by Jean Ann Lustberg and Phil Ra- 
mone (Teague both reads and sings on the 
set) , could become a very popular item. On 
the LP, as in the book, Teague talks to his in- 
fant son about the frustrations of a black man 
who "makes it" in white society. Arch Lust- 
berg produced the set.

RAKIN' AND SCRAPIN' - Harold Mabern - 
Prestige PRST 7624 
Harold Mabern, on piano and electric piano, 
serves up a splendid set of five jazz tunes, 
four of which he wrote, including the title 
track. The artist performs with sparkling 
grace and elan, and he receives topnotch sup- 
port from Blue Mitchell, trumpet: George 
Coleman, tenor sax; Bill Lee, bass; and Hugh 
Walker, drums. The cuts are "Rakin' And 
Scrapin'," "Such Is Life," "Aon," "I Heard 
It Through The Grapevine," and "Valerie." 
A jazz LP filled with good vibrations. 
A SOUL EXPERIMENT - Freddie Hubbar 
- Atlantic SD 1528 
Performing with colorful, economic 
splashes of sound, trumpeter Freddie Hubba 
paints a vivid jazz portrait of ten tunes. H 
lucid, bell -clear tones are heard to excelle 
advantage in such sessions as the title trac 
which Hubbard wrote in addition to two oth 
numbers; "Soul Turn Around: " "Clap 1b 
Hands; " and "South Street Stroll." Hubba 
is one of the finest trumpeters today, and iì 
outlets would do well to stock up on this 
hum.

Coin Car Wash Show 
Seen Biggest to Date 
CHICAGO - Response by leading 
laundry-drycleaning and coin carwash 
equipment manufacturers and suppli- 
ers to exhibit at the National Coin -Op 
Convention indicates a new record of 
over 30,000 square feet of exhibit space. 
Over 5E% of all space was applied for 
as of May 1. 
"When the 1969 Convention -Exhibit 
convenes in Chicago at the Conrad Hil- 
ton Hotel, October 16-18, there should 
be about 200 exhibitors displaying just 
about every classification 
of equip- 
ment, products and services for the 
coin -op laundry-drycleaning and coin 
carwash industries," stated Ward A. 
Gill, executive secretary of both the 
National 
Automatic 
Laundry 
and 
Cleaning Council (NALCC) and Na- 
tional Coin Carwash Council (NCCC) . 
Exhibits will be in the East-West 
and North halls on the lower level and 
Continental Room at the Hilton Hotel. 
This year the entire Continental Room 
will be devoted to exhibits and joined 
to the lower level with a battery of 
connecting escalators. 
It is urged that all exhibitors send 
in their space applications as soon as 
possible as maximum usage of all 
areas is predicted. Space assignments 
begin being made on June 1. 
Operator Guide Book 
As in past years, the NALCC-NCCC 
will provide the annual buyers Guide 
Book free to all operators and distribu- 
tors. Only exhibitors have the privi- 
lege of having their materials inser- 
ted in this year -around catalog refe- 
rence manual. The Guide Book has be- 
come one of the most important equip- 
ment and supply product manuals in 
the industry. It not only serves as a 
Convention time "hot list" to exhibits, 
but is used throughout the 1969-1970 
year as a guide to operators and dis- 
tributors in selecting new and replace- 
ment equipment. This year it will also 
serve as a year -around reference for 
prospective operators and investors. 
With 
Vari -Target, 
players 
man- 
aging to manipulate the balls to hit 
the special bumpers 
(a demanding 
skill feature) can boost the score 
from 10 to 500 points, depending upon 
the force with which the ball strikes. 
"Now in 
a four -player game, 
the 
unique feature should enable opera- 
tors here and abroad to insure maxi- 
mum earnings out of their dollars 
spent for new equipment," Gottlieb 
added. 
The overall cabinet and appearance 
of 'College Queens' is striking. Highly 
stylized artwork in the backglass de- 
picts campus cutie pies in some very 
mod outfits. What appear to be four 
"big men on campus- in a walking 
race, carry the lighted numbers on 
the chests (1-2-3-4) which signal the 
number of table players eligible. 
The color is great throughout. Gen- 
eral look 
of the playfield 
is 
un- 
cluttered and plenty of open space 
is provided 
to insure that proper 
attention to the Vari -Target feature 
can be given. 
Samples of the 
new 
four -player 
should be arriving at all D. Gottlieb 
& Co. distributors this week and the 
piece should be available for operator 
purchase at this reading. The factory 
expects heavy sales from the Euro- 
pean market where four -player pins 
are most popular of all.

MACKENNA'S GOLD - Music From The Mo- 
tion Picture Score - RCA Victor LSP 4096 
Jose Feliciano sings for the first time in a 
movie in Carl Foreman's "Mackenna's Gold," 
a Columbia Pictures presentation, starring 
Gregory Pack and Omar Sharif. Feliciano per- 
forms the theme song, "Ole Turkey Buzzard," 
in both Spanish and English. A surging, dyna- 
mic score was composed and conducted by 
Quincy Jones (an Oscar nominee for his "In 
Cold Blood" original score). Feliciano's char- 
acteristically strong performance, the big 
name cast, and Jones' fine score add up to a 
powerful sales package.

THE ANDERS & PONCIA ALBUM - Warner

Bros./Seven Arts WS 1778 
Pete Anders and Vinnie Poncia make their 
album debut as a rock duo with this offering. 
Of the 11 tunes on the LP, Anders & Poncia 
penned ten, including "I'm Beginning To 
Touch You," a light-hearted bit of hometown

uberant "Make A Change (To Something Bet- 
ter) ." Also on the set is the old Coasters' hit,

& Poncia off to a successful disk career. 
RUNNING JUMPING STANDING STILL -

BMI To Give 
Award For Best 
Job Film Score 
NEW YORK - BMI (Broadcast Mu- 
sic. Inc.) will give a special award to 
the writers of the best musical score 
of the more than 250 films which have 
been entered in the Job Film Fair 
competition at New York's Americana 
Hotel, May 21 and 22. The announce- 
ment was made jointly by Edward M. 
Cramer, BMI president, and Theodore 
W. Kheel, president of the American 
Foundation on Automation and Em- 
ployment, sponsor of the fair, the first 
international film festival on jobs, job 
training and the ghetto. 
Entries 
in the competition have 
been made by community organiza- 
tions, industry, unions, educational in- 
stitutions, groups and 
organizations 
concerned with public affairs, Govern- 
ment agencies and film producers. 
Entires have 
been 
received 
from 
Puerto Rico, Canada and Great Brit- 
ain, in addition to the United States. 
Final judging will be conducted dur- 
ing the two-day film fair. The judges 
will inclade representatives of ghetto 
youth and the hard-core unemployed, 
the business community, union lead- 
ers, educators and film producers. 
The event will be climaxed by a 
banquet to be keynoted by the Honor- 
able Winton W. Blount, United States 
Postmaster General, on May 22, at 
the Americana Hotel.

Producer's Profile 
CREED TAYLOR 
"It's pop if it sells, its jazz if it doesn't 
sell," is the way Creed Taylor looks at to- 
day's disk output from artists who were 
once relegated to a dusty bin at the back 
of the store. "They (the record 
com- 
panies) are trying to merchandise a jazz 
LP as a pop LP because the initial sales 
are better, and if the buyer thinks he's 
buying a pop album, that's what he'll 
hear when he gets home." 
"I deliberately try to put the jazz artist 
into a context that will hopefully be pop, 
without diluting what the artist does best. 
I don't try to change his particular thing, 
I just try to put it into a more broadly 
attractive atmosphere." 
Creed Taylor's philosophy towards jazz 
has helped many artists emerge from 
the confining strictures of categorization, 
and has provided many hit albums for 
the record companies he's worked for. 
His first album, a 10" LP produced for 
Bethlehem around 1953, was also his 
first success. The set, "Chris Conner 
Sings Lullabies 
Of 
Birdland," was 
a 
250,000 copy seller. 
It should be pointed out that Creed's 
aim is not to turn out hit albums, but to 
broaden the appeal of an artist he thinks 
is worthy of more attention. Under his 
independent, exclusive deal with 
A&R 
Records, Taylor turns out 15 albums a 
year, and he handles them all with love 
and care, sometimes spending a 
full 
week on remix alone. 
After gaining experience 
at 
Bethle 
hem, cutting Kai Winding and J. J. John- 
son and Herbie Mann, Taylor moved to 
ABC -Paramount. "I was feeling my way 
for awhile and trying to build a standard 
catalogue. 
I 
cut everything, 
drinking 
songs, 
war ballads, polkas, 
flamenco 
. 
I did one album you can still get by 
ordering from the back pages of moo 
ster magazines. It was called "Shock" 
Finally, 
I thought we were strong enough 
and 
I decided to go ahead with jazz pro- 
duct. The result was the Impulse jan 
line, 
the first 
high -quality 
packaged 
(gatefold covered) jazz line.

NEW YORK -A new record produc- 
tion company, Calmedia Productions, 
has been formed by Mal Williams, 
personal manager for Lynn Kellogg, 
Sam Taylor, Jr. 
and Al Thomas. 
Williams announced that the new com- 
pany's artists will be joint stock- 
holders 
with 
him, 
sharingin 
the 
firm's financial success. 
Williams simultaneously set up with 
the artists the original music publish- 
ing companies of Kellanwill Music 
Inc. (ASCAP) , and Allynsam Music 
Associate, 
Inc. 
(BMI) . 
The 
same 
financial arrangements will prevail. 
He also retained his own management 
firm of Mal Williams Associates, Inc. 
at 104 East 40th Street. 
Aside from the values derived from 
their ownership, Miss Kellogg, Taylor 
and Thomas will benefit profession- 
ally from the new ventures, Williams 
said. He added: 
"The companies will maintain 
a 
staff of writers and arrangers supply- 
ing ideas geared to their individual 
needs and talents, and also will be in 
position to rehearse as frequently as 
required with 
the artists, insuring 
total preparation in all possible areas." 
Miss Kellogg, the original female 
lead of "Hair" on Broadway, has 
appeared 
on 
seven 
television 
pro- 
grams thus far in 1969. She recently 
made 
her 
motion -picture 
debut in 
"Carro" 
with 
Elvis 
Presley 
for 
National General Pictures, and has a 
multi -picture deal with the studio. She 
also is featured in Royal Crown Cola, 
Gillette Techmatic, and Salem Ciga- 
rette commercials. 
She will next be seen on television 
on the "Jonathan Winters Show" on 
CBS May 8th, and she has just taped 
a segment with John Davidson 
in 
London for his summer series. 
Taylor is a blues singer, composer, 
arranger and producer. He will record 
his own material, and produce many 
of the sessions himself. 
Due for release from the Army this 
month after two years of service, 
Thomas is a guitarist, composer and

EASTERN FLASHES 
HOPPIN' AT THE HILTON - Well, 
by now it's all over but the hangovers. 
Since we go to press the preceding 
Thursday, full story on the Al Denver 
(JA) testimonial bash won't be car- 
ried till next week, but at press time, 
all the data pointed to a real terrific 
time for the jukebox trade as they 
celebrated the successful windup of 
the 1969 life saving campaign. Dona- 
tion pledges were sure to mount to 
$30,000 mark (all pledged to our in- 
dustry) and ticket reservations were 
nearing SRO. At the last executive 
committee meeting, chairman 
Gil 
Sonin thanked all those who had faith- 
fully attended the numerous confer- 
ences that coordinated this year's 
drive and victory dinner planning. Gil 
once again made mention of the short 
time we had to get things tied up this 
year, owing to that maddening snow- 
storm as well as a brief but telling 
UJA clerical workers strike. Special 
thanks for hard work on the com- 
mittee this year go to: Gil, Ben Chi- 
cofsky, Lou Wolbeg, Max Klein, Max 
Weiss, Marty Herbshman, Bernie An- 
tonoff (who will show up with his 
own cigarettes next year!) , Sam Mor- 
rison, Harold Kaufman, Carl Pavesi, 
Meyer Parkoff, Abe Lipsky, and of 
course guest of honor Al Denver and 
UJA execs George Nemzoff and Walt 
Lasker. 
AROUND TOWN - Also at the Hilt- 
on last week were I.Q. Computer chief 
Gene Wagner, exhibiting his game 
at the Shopping Center show. Gene 
info'd he may have a startling an- 
nouncement for the trade in a few 
weeks. Curiously enough, while Wag- 
ner entertained his customers that 
Monday evening, Lou Wolberg and 
Abe Lipsky were also in the hotel 
at the same time meeting with ex- 
otic dancer Irene Dawson in the lob- 
by to give her necessary details on 
the UJA show where she wat to en- 
tertain. Never meeting before, the 
two distribs carried a copy of Cash 
Box so she'd recognize them. Come 
on, fellas, didn't you ever hear of 
a green carnation? 
ON THE STREET - Al 
Simon 
at Simon distributing receiving some 
California tradesmen last week, bub- 
bled over with stories sent back by 
Len Schneller about the Bi -State 8 - 
ball meet in Davenport. See details 
elsewhere on the two-day finals. Mean- 
while, Al D'Inzillo at the Simon show- 
room (an accomplished small craft 
pilot) says he's not getting in much 
flying these days since he has to drive 
from his Nassau County home clear 
up to the White Plains Airport where 
he rents the planes and the traveling 
takes up half hisSaturdays. Besides, 
he says it's more fun and actually 
safer to fly during the winter months 
Harry Green and Sam Morrison 
puzzling over some interesting art- 
work over at Runyon's which Sam 
had purchased at a Broadway gal- 
lery. Didn't know you guys appre- 
ciated fine art! Over at Lipsky's, 
some of the visiting operators were 
embroiled in a cultural discussion on 
the enterprising attitudes of some 
Gypsies. You can learn a lot on the 
street.

hope you all can get out there. Vic re-

New York Guild meetings upstate and 
info's the lads enjoyed a terrific show 
after the business was 
completed.

Blue Thumb Sales 
Under John Nelson 
HOLLYWOOD - John 
Nelson has 
been named to the post of director of 
national sales for Blue Thumb Rec- 
ords, 
according 
to 
president 
Bob 
Krasnow. 
Nelson was most recently area man- 
ager for Philco-Ford Corp., working 
out of Philadelphia. He has also serv- 
ed as office manager for Privilege 
Dist. in L. A., branch manager for 
Privilege Dist. in San Francisco, sales 
representative for Hart Dist. in L. A. 
and manager of the record dept. of 
G. Schirmer, Inc. in L. A. 
Gray To W. Coast For 
York -Pala Publishing 
NEW YORK - Charles Greene, presi- 
dent of York -Pala Records, has an- 
nounced the appointment of Norman 
Gray as west coast publishing co- 
ordinator for 10 -East Music 
(BMI) , 
5 -West 
Music 
(BMI), 
5th 
Avenue 
Music (ASCAP) and subsidiary pub- 
lishing interests assembled under the 
banner of Greene/Stone Enterprises. 
Gray, who developed The Brooklyn 
Candy Store chain and its national 
franchise operation, will also become 
directly involved in the development 
of material, artists and supervision 
of composer contractees. Gray re- 
ports directly to Gail Wallis, General 
Manager of Greene/Stone Publishing 
complex. 
6th BMI Showcase 
Underway This Week 
NEW YORK - For the sixth year, 
BMI is presenting its annual Musical 
Theater Workshop Showcase to in- 
vited audiences at New York's New 
Theatre. 
Three 
one -hour 
perfor- 
mances - May 20, 27 and June 3 - 
introduced by Lehman Engel, director 
of the Workshop, will feature the 
works of a number of aspiring musi- 
cal theater talents. 
BMI's Musical Theater Workshop 
offers regular sessions in New York, 
and, beginning this season, in Los 
Angeles, to composers and lyricists 
for the musical theater. All costs for 
the Workshop are borne by BMI, and 
students who make progress may con- 
tinue indefinitely. Each spring, many 
of their works are performed by pro- 
fessional actors before invited audi- 
ences of theatrical producers, music 
publishers, the press and other pro- 
fessionals. 
The Workshop was established by 
BMI in 1960, and is designed to stimu- 
láte proven writers and to develop 
new talent for the musical theater.

MOTOR -CYCLE - Lotti Golden - Atlantic 
SD 8223 
Lotti Golden could be one of the next big 
femme singer/writers, and her debut album 
should do particularly well in underground 
areas. 
Lark's 
autobiographical 
tale 
of 
changes, as arranged and produced by Bob 
Crewe, is an explosive pop happening which 
is already garnering heavy airplay and under- 
ground comment. "Motor -Cycle Michael" and 
"Get Together (With Yourself) " are top cuts 
here, but every track offers a new listening 
experience. 
DIAL -A -HIT - Various Artists - Bell 6030 
Purchasers of Bell Records' "Dial -A -Hit" 
disk can dial hit numbers by the Box Tops 
("The Letter") , Bobby Russell ("1432 Franklin 
Pike Circle Hero") , James & Bobby Purify 
("Shake A Tail Feather") , and Merrilee Rush 
("Angel Of The Morning") . Heavy sellers by 
the Delphonics ("La -La Means I Love You") 
and Al Greene ("Back Up Train") also contri- 
bute to an album that is likely to itself prove 
a fast-moving sales item. 
BUDDAH'S 
360° 
DIAL -A -HIT - Various 
Artists - Buddah BDS 5039 
A 360 -degree dial graces the cover of this 
album of Buddah singles, many of which hit 
the charts, and the listener can thus both spin 
the dial and the disk. (The dial includes 
photos of the various acts.) Featured on the 
LP are such strong items as "Indian Giver," 
1910 Fruitgum Co.; "Worst That Could Hap- 
pen," Brooklynt Bridge; "Mercy," Ohio Ex- 
press; and "Summer In The City," Lovin' 
Spoonful. Recently pacted Buddah artists 
Melanie, Elephants Memory, and U.S. '69 
are also represented. Could be a big sales 
flurry here. 
DEPARTURE - Pat Boone - Tetragramma- 
ton T 118 
A few dashes of funkiness have been added 
to Pat Boone's style, which accounts for his 
"Departure." His latest set, which is a mix- 
ture of contemporary and country, includes 
songs by Tim Buckley, John D. Loudermilk, 
Biff Rose, Fred Neil and John Stewart, among 
others, and is a very listenable effort which 
could appeal to a wide audience. Keep an eye 
on it. 
YOU GOTTA TAKE A LITTLE LOVE - 
Horace Silver Quintet - Blue Note BST 84309 
The Horace Silver Quintet performs, with

DON PARTRIDGE - STREET BUSKER -

A street busker (from the verb "busk," to 
move or shift about restlessly) is a street 
musician and a sort of one-man band. A 
busker's equipment might include a guitar, 
a drum, cymbal, tambourine, kazoo, and har 
monica. On this album, British street busker

add Arthur Otley) ," from the film "Otley, and 
"Rosie," are highspots on the set. A mou

Gospel music showing an increase 
in Canada, much of it due to the re- 
cent chart success of "Oh Happy 
Day by the Edwin Hawkins Singers 
on Pavilion. The Ralph Carmichael 
LP "Looked For Love" now chalking 
up good sales. Light Records is a 
division of Lexicon Music, Vancouver. 
One of Canada's top West Coast 
groups, the Collectors, have suffered 
somewhat through the split of their 
lead singer Howie Vickers who has 
apparently left the group to go it 
alone. Their Warner Bros./New Syn- 
drome LP "Grass And Wild Straw- 
berries" has done exceptionally well 
for them. They have also become 
much sought after for Canadian and 
V. S. tours, having recently played to 
good houses at New York's Fillmore 
East, Detroit's Grande Ballroom, the 
Ark in Boston and Scene in New York. 
They also drew capacity houses at the 
Jubilee in Edmonton. Expo '70 will 
feature music by the Collectors in the 
Canadian Pavilion. 
The highly successful Polydor vocal 
group, the Sceptres, release "Good 
Morning New Day,' written by Ar- 
lene King and Ellen Star of the South- 
ern Music group, arranged by Herb 
Bernstein and produced by Montreal's 
Bob Hahn. The flip is a Johnny Cowell 
penning of "Walk Hand In Hand." 
Also from Polydor comes the old Dave 
Guard outing of "Scotch And Soda" 
by the Kingston Trio. (Tetragramma- 
ton in U. S.) . Another Tetragramma- 
ton single, released on Polydor in 
Canada,. making a large -sized noise 
is the Elyse Weinberg lid of "Oh 
Deed I Do." Hot on the heels of their 
single success of "Moody Morning 
Blues" comes the Five Bells' first 
LP release "Dimensions." Initial re- 
action with MOR stations has been 
impressive. 
Much action happening for Cana- 
dian product from the Compo Com- 
pany. Buckstone Hardware receiving 
national play with their lid of "Pack 
It In" 
on 
Apex; 
Dionne 
Brooks' 
"Walkin' On My Mind" showing good 
national gains as is another Revolver 
release of "When I Die" by Mother - 
lode. The latter is being successfully 
touted by the Martin Onrot P. R. 
firm who arranged for delivery of the 
disc by Brinks Express to local radio 
and press people. The big promotion 
going on at Compo is the Roger 
Williams Month which has created 
much interest in the complete catalog 
of the Kapp recording star. Compo 
rush released Williams' latest LP 
"Happy Heart" which received al- 
most instantaneous play at MOR sta- 
tions across Canada. Also shaping up 
to be a successful outing for Williams 
is his single of "Galveston" which has 
even caught the ear of the "progres- 
sive rock" stations. New Apex release 
by Michel Louvain, "Une Rose Au 
Coeur," produced by Yvan Dufresne 
catching fire in Quebec. Lavern Baker 
release, on Brunswick, a Ray Griff 
penning of "Baby." Griff, a native of 
Calgary, now living in Nashville.

Trend Records of Canada located 
in West Hill, Ont., showing promise 
of becoming major production and 
pressing centre. The complex, bossed 
by Mery Buchanan and Dutch under- 
ground folk -singer Guido Smit, was 
built by Buchanan in co-operation 
with Pete Traynor, operator of York- 
ville Sound Ltd., and contains multi- 
track facilities. Trend is currently 
pressing and distributing product for 
the Ontario/Quebec market. Releases

rently producing a single and an LP 
for Toronto's Cargo for release the 
latter part of May.

Vogue Records is launching a new 
series of records in France. This col- 
lection is titled Double Loisirs and it 
offers a two LP set for the cost of 
one: 24, 45 FF. Two sets are already 
on release. The first is called "Les 
Geants du Jazz" and offers a very in- 
teresting jazz anthology presenting 
namely Armstrong, Basie, Ellington, 
Charlie Parker, Gerry Mulligan, Monk, 
Kid Ory. The second set is devoted to 
Napoleon and contains the love letters 
of Bonaparte to Josephine.

Reprise group, Vogue releases this

of June 7th for a Musicorama gala.

Andy Miele Heads Sales At Polydoi 
Talent On Stage 
TOM JONES 
COPACABANA, N. Y. - Tom Jones 
is a remarkable composite of the 
power of many things: the carryover 
of the blues idiom into all segments of 
our society; the new sexual freedom 
and the potent hand of TV in the crea- 
tion of a super star. 
Lest this clinical approach to the 
young Welshman seem too detached, 
let it be said that his opening night 
performance at the Copacabana last 
Thursday (22) was a night to remem- 
ber. Only the Beatles - and their ap- 
peal at the start was limited to little 
more than teeny-boppers - have el- 
icited the squeals and swoon -like re- 
sponse from an audience in recent 
years. Women who may have brought 
their children along show no less en- 
thusiasm for Jones' kinetic, pelvic 
(his gyrations make the old Presley 
five year olds). Who but Lyndon John- 
son, the Mets and Mickey Mantle 
have been honored by placards over 
the past few years? Add Tom Jones, 
thanks to some girls from the S&H 
greenstamps company who waved the 
sign ("We Love You Tom") during 
his performance and got a chance to 
show it to the London disk artist in 
his dressing room after the show. 
Beneath all this - and the excite- 
ment that surrounds him does require 
probing - is a voice of iron, yet supple 
in response to rhythm and sentiment. 
Perhaps most of all, Tom Jones uses 
his vocal equipment to best advan- 
tage, seemingly for his own fulfillment 
and the hungry, eager needs of his 
fans. He is a master on knowing how 
not to let his fans down. The image 
that Jones has created on TV is no 
trick of the video art. It's all there 
plus a lot more in real -life.

Rosica Dot VP 
LOS ANGELES - John Rosica has 
been elected vice-president of promo- 
tion and artist relations at Dot Re- 
cords, reports Arnold Burk, Para- 
mount Pictures Corp. vice-president 
in charge of music operations and 
president of Dot Records. Rosica pre- 
viously served the company as Direc- 
tor of Promotion and Merchandising. 
with this new appointment," 
'Burk said, "we are not only express- 
ing our. confidence in John Rosica 
and in the new national promotion 
structure instituted in our company. 
We are recognizing the promotion and 
artist relations functions as vital, 
primary concerns of our company - 
on a par with the areas of sales dis- 
tribution, A & R, and advertising mer- 
chandising, all of which are headed by 
company vice presidents." 
Rosica began his career in 1956 as a 
staff announcer with WHAT Radio, 
Philadelphia. Shortly thereafter he 
joined WIP as their music director. 
In early 1958 he made his way into the 
record industry as a sales -promotion 
man with Lesco Distributors. He was 
tapped by RCA Victor in 1959, func- 
tioning as a regional promotion man, 
also in Philly. Two years later he was 
upped to a regional promotion post in 
New York. Subsequently Rosica was 
elevated to National Promotion Man- 
ager, also responsible for artist rela- 
tions. 
In July of 1967 Rosica accepted a 
position as director of product for 
Creed Taylor, Inc., a division of A & M 
Records, where he helmed merchandis- 
ing and promotion. He joined Dot in 
January of this year.

Coleman Hawkins Dies At 64 
NEW YORK - Coleman Hawkins, 
one of America's jazz greats for more 
than forty years, died last Monday 
(19) 
of pneumonia at Wickersham 
Hospital in N. Y. Hawkins, billed as 
the "Father of the tenor sax" was 64. 
Born in St. Joseph, Mo., he arrived 
in N. Y. as a member of Mamie 
Smith's Jazz Hounds, cutting his first 
sides with Fletcher Henderson's band 
in 1923. In 1933 he formed his own 
combo, featuring Henry (Red) Allen 
on trumpet, Horace Henderson 
on 
piano and J. C. Higginbotham on 
bass. In '39 he recorded his most 
famous sessions for the 
Bluebird 
label. They included "She's Funny 
That Way," "Meet Dr. Foo" and 
"Body and 
Soul" 
which 
was 
a 
million seller. Throughout the years, 
it was his most requested title. 
Frequent trips to Europe estab- 
lished him as an international jazz 
figure. A lush warm style, marked by 
sweeping 
legato 
phrases was 
his 
trademark. During the 40's and 50's 
he toured with his own small group 
and was heard on the Jazz at the 
Philharmonic sides cut by Norman 
Grantz. 
Hawkins placed #1 on all the Esquire 
Jazz polls held and was generally 
#1 tenor sax soloist on the Playboy, 
Downbeat and Metronome polls. 
He leaves a rich legacy of his 
talents on such labels as Apollo, Key- 
note, Victor, HMV, CMS, Savoy and 
Capitol.

Bobby Short, savior to long -lost gems 
of the musical theatre and any song 
worth its salt, is not a loss for things 
to do these days. He's just finished 
the second of two concerts with Mabel 
Mercer at Carnegie Hall, where, by 
the way, he lives in an adjoining apart- 
ment. Last Tuesday, he cut his first 
commercial, for the new Restaurant 
Associates eatery in New York, Spatz. 
Indicative of his feeling that he's get- 
ting broader recognition than he's 
ever had is the happy fact that when 
the ad guys heard the Spatz jingle 
the first performer who came to 
mind who could do the item justice 
was 
"Bobby 
Short! " 
Bobby, 
the 
nightly guardian of good music at 
the 
Carlisle, 
is 
presently 
adding 
sessions for an upcoming Atlantic 
LP, tentatively titled "New York's 
My Personal Property." It'll include 
some new numbers and, to the de- 
light of his fans, some obscure songs 
from the past. Bobby doesn't hide 
his own delight at the number of 
people who drop by to say hello 
when he's lunching. "After 25 years 
as an entertainer, it's nice to know 
I'm finally on a lot of peoples minds." 
be beams. Much of the current com-

feature story in the Sunday Times." 
In truth, Bobby's always been 
a 
household name to all who realize 
that there's more to Irvine Berlin 
than "There's No Business Like Show 
Business." 
FOCUS ON JAZZ 
One sure way to be reminded that 
about a year has gone by again is the 
release of a new Horace Silver album. 
"You Gotta Take A Little Love" is the 
name of his latest and, as usual, it's 
on Blue Note. I guess that Horace and 
Blue Note have been blissfully mar- 
ried to one another as long as any art- 
ist and company that come to mind. 
Of course, any union prospers better 
in success than it does in mediocrity 
or failure, and Horaces's albums have 
always enjoyed great success, both 
from the critics and from the story 
told by record sales. Much of this suc- 
cess must be attributed to the fact that 
Horace's albums are as infrequent as 
they are, and that when he and his col- 
leagues go into the studio to record, 
things are really together. 
Brotherhood Theme 
Seven of the eight compositions that 
comprise this new album are originals 
by Horace, and the theme for the al- 
bum is BROTHERHOOD. The eighth 
selection is one written by Bennie 
Maupin, Horace's new saxophone -flut- 
ist and is titled, "Lovely's Daughter". 
Unique to this release is the fact that 
Horace has also written lyrics to four 
of his seven compositions ... and the 
liner notes, as well. This is a full-blown 
Horace Silver production! 
I never cease to marvel at how Silver 
can continue to find new players who 
are able to perpetuate that character- 
istic Horace Silver "oonka choonka" 
sound, the sound that has made it 
comparatively easy to identify as Hor- 
ace's. True, the community of jazz 
musicians is ripe with capable young 
players, but to be able to weld them 
into a group with such a personal 
sound is another thing and the fact 
that Horace continues to be able to do 
so with each change of personnel is a 
distinct tribute to his talent as a 
leader. 
Usual Silver Pacing 
As usual, Silver has exercised his 
good judgment. Programming on this 
new album is a succession of shift- 
ing changes and colors. Tempos vary, 
moods differ, and, as a consequence, 
one's interest remains intact. I believe 
that as much as anyone else, Horace 
Silver has learned the art of maintain- 
ing his audience's span of attention. 
Anyone would agree That without that 
span of attention boredom would be- 
come a quick replacement, especially 
in jazz where improvisation is so much 
a part of things and where lengthy ex- 
plorations become more and more 
common. Of special note, too, is the 
playing of Horace's new drummer, 
Billy Cobham, Jr., who, like all Horace 
Silver drummers before him, has been 
able to provide precisely what is need- 
ed to compliment Horace's playing and 
his writing. Each time Silver comes 
up with a new drummer I ask myself 
the same question, "Where does he 
find them?" Lest you believe that I'm 
less impressed by the other new mem- 
bers of the group, let me dispel that 
idea at once. The front line of Randy 
MORT FEGA 
Brecker and Bennie Maupin does ye 
man service as does bassist John W 
liams. I can't help thinking about tl 
days when Horace joined Art Blakey

RCA Names Fred Ruppert 
NY Field Promotion Rep 
NEW YORK - Fred Ruppert has been 
named by RCA Records to the post of 
New York field promotion represen- 
tative. 
Reporting to Frank O'Donnell, man- 
ager of sales and promotion for the 
eastern district, Ruppert is responsible 
for radio airplay of RCA product in the 
New York area as well as radio and 
television promotion of artists when 
they visit the same region. 
Twenty-six year old Ruppert joined 
RCA Records in March of .1968 as the 
field promotion representative for the 
state of Florida. A graduate of the 
University of Miami, Ruppert had for- 
merly been a record buyer for Jordan 
Marsh in Florida, as well as general 
merchandise manager for Foremost 
Sales Promotions of Florida. 
adrb 
Fred Ruppert

Zenith Reveals '70 Line; 
4 Cassette Units Included 
CHICAGO - Zenith Radio Corp. has 
marked its entry into the portable 
cassette tape recorder business with 
the introduction of four cassette units 
in the 1970 line. Zenith last week took 
the wraps off 24 console hi-fi stereo 
players and 
a 
phonograph/AM-FM 
stereo -phonograph both featuring the 
company's modular 
stereo "Circle 
of Sound" system at lower suggested 
retail prices. 
Describing several of the new engi- 
neering developments featured in the 
'70 line, Walter Fisher, president of 
Zenith Sales Co., highlighted an ad- 
vanced design 'Custom Stereo Pro- 
fessional' 
4 -speed 
record 
changer 
with synchronized motor drive; a new 
'instant touch' stereo control panel 
with six control buttons which are 
highly sensitive and light up when 
touched to control a mode of opera- 
tion; and a solid-state AM -FM -Stereo 
FM radio with new field effect transis- 
tor circuit. 
Seventeen consoles in Zenith's line 
have two exponential horns, plus a 
total of either four or six woofers and 
hi-fi cone -type tweeters in the sound 
system. Amplifiertuner systems in the 
consoles are completely solid-state and 
deliver either 32, 60, 
100, 140 or 320 
watts of peak music power. Manufac- 
turer's suggested retail prices of the 
console 
series range 
from 
$199.95 
to $575.00. Two models have no sug- 
gested retail price. 
Cassette Tape Units 
The four models premiered as Zenith's 
first cassette units are: the Nomad 
(A602) player: three player/recorders 
named the Classmate 
(A608) 
, 
Duet 
(A6I0) and Interlude (A625) which also 
features an 
AM -FM radio built-in. 
All four units operate of standard 'D' 
cell batteries (not included in the pur- 
chase price) . 
Retail prices suggested are $19.95 
for the Nomad, $49.95 for the Class- 
mate, $59,95 for the Duet and $99.95 
for the Interlude. 
Expanding its tape facilities, Zenith 
is also offering instrument accept- 
ance in many units for 4 -track cassette 
tape stereo recorders that drop -in 
or operate on top of the master con- 
sole unit. Priced at $99.95 is the drop - 
in player/recorder model A632. The 
"slave" unit (A636W) has no suggest- 
ed retail price.

will 
be 
holding 
open 
houses and local showings of the com-

Cassette Tapes In 
New Expansion Move 
NEW 
YORK - "Every yardstick 
points to cassettes as the burgeoning 
tape market," noted Robins Industries 
Corp.'s president Herman Post in his 
announcement 
that 
the 
firm 
will 
undertake a major expansion into the 
magnetic tape -cassette field. Robins 
is known for its open -reel tape and 
accessory devices, and Post said that 
there are special production facilities 
now being installed for cassette pro- 
ducts. 
"Our objective," he stated, "is to 
become 
the 
major 
single 
source 
of all kinds of recording tape and re- 
lated products, with particular empha- 
sis on cassettes and cassette -accessory 
devices." 
In addition to pointing its attention 
at cassette equipment, Robins has 
found that the configuration -generated 
interest has "helped reel-to-reel busi- 
ness."
