Cash Box — June 6, 1970

---- p42
insigM&soundcontinued
NEW YORK - (Con’t from page 41)
real
I'm doing
it my way. The thing about
large record companies
is that most
couldn't care less about music or people; you’re
a cipher distinguished from
all
the other ciphers
solely by how much money you're
bringing
in.
That's why
I
picked
Bell to distribute Windfall. You're an individual there; they care about what
you're trying to do.”
Along with Windfall, whose business end
is largely handled by Bud Prager, came
Felix’s group, Mountain: born
in
late August,
1969. They opened
in Ungano’s
in
New York after about ten days of being together. Immediately after came a rather
mediocre semi-solo album by Leslie West. By October Mountain had found a new
drummer, Corky Laing, and rehearsals began
in earnest. "We now have a genuine
family unit playing together,"
Felix told me
late
in December, during a recording
session break. “This was the first Christmas
I didn’t spend with my family;
I spent
it with my musical family.”
Out of these sessions spanning four months (Nov-Feb) came “Mountain Climb-
ing!" Painstaking care went into every phase of
its creation, not only
in laying down
the tracks, but in mixing, stereo separation, and the actual placement of the songs
on the record disk. The LP
itself deserves some discussion
in that
it may be the
most important album
in
Felix’s career. Undoubtedly Mountain, as
a group,
will
make better ones, but for Felix, personally, “Climbing!”
is a turning point.
“I believe
so strongly in this project, that
if
it doesn't sell
I’ll pack
it
in,” Felix told me during
the early part of the sessions.
The first track, “Mississippi Queen,”
is Mountain with
its strictly American
roots
showing; a powerful, timeless song of youth
in much the same way as Leon Rus-
sell’s “Delta Lady.” Of Jack Bruce’s “Theme
For An Imaginary Western,” the next
song, Felix says
"I’ll never re-do a song again" (he produced an earlier version for
Jack on
his solo
LP).
Nevertheless Mountain’s version
is superior
in every
way.
Felix’s achingly beautiful voice conjurs up perfectly the wide desolate plains of the
song, and bass, drums, organ, mellotron and guitar all contribute to the loneliness
of the Western wagoneers. “Never
In My
Life” expresses the family’s feelings
at
the sessions.
“For Yasgur’s Farm,” which
starts side two,
is
a major work. A duet between
Felix's smooth
light voice and
Leslie’s deep dark voice,
it has been
in Mountain's
live repertory since the beginning and
first showed where they were going. This
moves
into an acoustic instrumental by
Leslie. “People who said
Leslie sounded
like
Eric
(Clapton
of Cream)
just weren’t
listening very
closely.
This
track
will
prove
it to them," says
Felix. There’s just a
spiral from
this to "The
Laird,” softly
flowing on the bottom, sharp and crackling on top with
Leslie’s guitar to empha-
size
Felix's gently sung but stinging vocals.
After
a
Mountain-hard-rock break of
“Sittin’ On A Rainbow,” the album closes with “Boys
In The Band" also
a major
work and
Felix’s personal
favorite. To say that
it
is classically rooted would be
a
misrepresentation inasmuch as classical music
is so much a part of
Felix.
Every-
thing he does comes from
his mind and
his gut
(writing
is
a
visceral
act; good
writers write as they
feel). So the classics are always there with
him, extending
his range as a musician to infinity.
“Boys
In The Band”
is Chopin, and Bach;
it
is a rondo and a fugue;
it
is saying
goodbye and hello: a dance of death and
life;
it
is an ellipse, a never-ending cycle;
it is Mountain and
it is Felix Pappalardi.
eric van lustbader
Doctors Find Crimso Completely Well
One of the finest albums to come out of Britain last year was King Crimson’s "In
The Court of the Crimson King." And as a
first LP
it
is singular
in the new direc-
tions
in music
it explores. But after
its release and
a short tour of the
U.
S.,
re-
ports stated that the group was splitting up.
Crimso’s leader, Robert Fripp dropped
by
last week
to dispel any such
disas-
trous and unfounded rumors. The group
is indeed
alive and
thriving as witness
their new single “Catfood” and LP, "In the Wake of Poseidon.”
“‘Poseidon’
is the soundtrack for an imaginary film," says Bob. "The idea
is that
from the four elements, earth,
air, fire and water, you can get twelve personalities,
such as the warrior who
is fire and
earth. We personify these characters through
the music."
About Crimso’s personnel changes,
Fripp has this to say: "After the
U.
S. tour
we
split
into three
parts. Greg Lake
(vocalist) joined up with
Keith Emerson
(ex-
Nice); Mike Giles (drums) and Ian McDonald (mellotron) are playing with friends
of theirs and
I am
still here with Pete Sinfield, who does all the lyrics. Basically the
second album
is two people plus friends. What we want to do
is to build up a pool
of musicians to work together on our LP’s.”
“Poseidon”
is a direct progression from “Court." Like Mountain's music, Crimso's
is constantly growing, and therefore, constantly surprising; constantly invigorating.
It
is
total music because
it surrounds and
engulfs the
listener.
It
isn’t,
as Bob
would say, “tap your foot and nod your neck” music.
Upcoming for Crimso:
a
third
LP with
Keith Emerson and John
(Colosseum)
Hiseman,
a second
U.S. tour,
a cartoon made from the "Moonchild” track from
the "Court” LP, and
a film using the “Devil’s Triangle” cut from the new album.
Crimso is in bloom.
Long Short Takes
Talked with some good folks this week. One of them was Karen Wyman, the 17-
year-old
singing
sensation
(beware
of
yellow
journalism!).
Overnight
she
has
launched into a strong career in singing with dates set at the Sands (from June 3)
with Don Adams, and the Shamrock Hilton (from June 17) in Houston as the head-
liner. She’s already tucked a
lot of national TV time under her
belt,
too. Her
first
LP was released
last week by Decca, and provides her with
a
lot of enthusiastic
conversation matter — how the material
is so “now,” how she got what she wanted
in
a
strong,
brassy
instrumental
backing, and how much
she
likes
the
group,
Chicago. We talked a
little about acting, how she sees singing the same as acting,
how she has read for a few parts; and about her Life magazine six-page feature on
her that
is
still up
in the
air. School’s out so
you'll
be hearing a
lot more from
Karen.
Picked up on the staging techniques (among other things) of the Ace Trucking
Company the other day in an interview with the RCA improv comedy quintet. They
explained that they open the show with a suggestion period from the audience for
sketch
ideas. The group says this frees the audience's
inhibitions.
Unlike some
improv groups that work out
in theater surroundings and use improv as an acting
exercise, the Truckers make
it very clear that they work "purely for entertainment
using slapstick and cerebral comedy techniques" and
in saloon atmospheres or
college halls for drinkers and otherwise. Got a
lot of TV and concert action coming
up so be on the lookout for them. They’re a moving experience
(I couldn’t resist).

dustries’

11 divisions show-

Pic-

to $11,521,000, compared to $12,005,000
a year before. Sales were $415,775,000,
compared

$397,833,000.

$36,111,000.

Control Core Of Apple Success
(Con’t. from page 9)
day, Klein says,
is completely depen-
dent upon
“total
sovereignty.” Com-
plete
artistic
control,
control
of
the
release schedule, control of the quan-
tity
to be
shipped and
the
presenta-
tion of the
art. In Apple’s case, Klein
goes on, Apple masters
its own tapes,
ships the parts to the Capitol pressing
plant,
approves
test
pressings,
origi-
nates cover
art and
designs
its own
ads. “And we end up
with
only one
account receivable to a company with
a Triple A rating, Capitol.”
When an independent company has
complete
control
of
its
product
and
believes completely in the talent
it
is
featuring,
it has but two functions:
1)
to get exposure on the
air for
its
re-
lease; and 2) get the product into the
market place when
its
hot. For
pro-
motion,
of
course,
an
efficient
job
must be done at the distribution level.
When- Apple believed in
its product,
it
backed
its
releases
with
heavy
initial shipments. The initial shipment
on
John
Lennon’s
“Instant Karma”
single was
500,000
units. “On
an
un-
tried entity like ‘Come And Get
It’ by
Badfinger, we pressed up
250,000
ini-
tially. We did so because
the motion
picture
company
which
had
the
‘Magic
Christian’
in which the
single
was
featured,
bought
air
time
plug-
ging the single. On the ‘Let It Be’

Visits Far East
WALT WALDMAN
TOKYO -

of

recently
completed
an

which

visited

.
-
-
-
ft —
While, in Tokyo he met with SEGA’s

and
inspected
the
firm’s
production
facilities.

accompanied
by his wife Shirley,
also visited Expo
’70 where he viewed the coin-operated
machines
on
display.
Waldman
said the
fair was “much more
excit-
ing
and
impressive
than

seemed on U.S. television.”
Waldman
is
an

for
several

manufacturers.

EASTERN FLASHES
THE BAHAMA BASH —
It’s
all over but the memories now — great memories of a
long
Memorial
Day weekend
filled
to
overflowing
with
tropical
sun,
swimming,
gambling, shopping and
golf,
golf, and more
golf. Operators and
their
ladies from
all over the metro area agreed the 1970 combined-associations convention was
a
well-planned and coordinated weekend of activities. Planes went off pretty much on
time, and the
light
rain which
greeted
the “music
associates” group on
arrival
in
Freeport, Grand Bahama, dried up for good almost as soon as the planes touched
down,
leaving rosy weather from then on. From the rum
swizel
party
at the
Kings
Inn Thursday night, thru a sumptious farewell luncheon Sunday, everything clicked
thanks to prior planning on the part of Ben Chicofsky, George Holtzman and Sophie
Selinger. Only
negative
note was the vastness
of the
Kings
Inn
itself,
which
had
some of our people
lost
in the crowd
looking for the
rest
of the group. Some
of
those from the operating trade who made the
trip included
association
leaders
Al
Denver,
Carl
Pavesi, Jack Wilson, Mike Mulqueen,
operators
Sal
Trella,
Lou
Levy,
Jack
Miller,
Bill
Fritz,
Nash
Gordon,
Bernie
Antonoff,
Lou
Tartaglia, Max
Weiss,
Casper La Marca, Lou Valenti, Abe Weisberg, Al
Kress, Sam Schwartz, Marty Herb-
shman and Tony and
Bill LaMorte. Attorneys Teddy
Blatt and Malcolm Wein were
also there. Record company execs
included
Mort Hoffman
of
Epic,
Paul Smith
of
Columbia,
Phil Wesson
of London and Marv
Paris of Decca. Columbia,
incidentally,
took a
hospitality suite at the Kings
Inn where they entertained the ops. They also
brought in recording group called Pacific Gas & Electric to "meet the guys".
HERE AND THERE — The New York State Operators Guild
will hold
its next meeting
June
17th
at the Governor Clinton
Hotel
in
Kingston. Meet gets underway
at the
standard 7:30 PM hour
.
.
. Center of attraction at the Broadway Arcade (52nd
St.)
is Allied
Leisure's brand new
‘Wild
Cycle’ race game.
Unit
arrived
last Wed.
at
Al
Simon’s, was promptly uncrated and trucked over to their fun
center
to meet the
Broadway arcade crowd.
Unit, operates on quarter
play,
tests the
player's
skill
to
maneuver the motorcycle down the
rolling road
(via
authentic handle
bars, com-
plete with speed control).
It also bangs out rock music via stereo cartridge,
putting
the player in that “easy rider” mood. Real fun, and according to Allied’s sales man-
ager Gene
Lipkin,
sure
to
book
record
collections.
Report from
one
location,
a
Florida skating rink, had the cash pot up to $82
in
less than ten hours of a Saturday,
Gene says, which
is nothing short of phenominal
.
.
. Brunswick Corp’s pool table
/,
sales reps are convened this week at the Marion, Va. table factory,
for annual con-
ference. Part of the week's activities
will include a detailed tour of the table assem-
bly line, according to coin table sales chief Mac MaKenny, giving the lads a more
in-
tensive knowledge
of the product they
are
representing
before the
U.S.
operating
trade
.
.
.
Metro New York games ops
are
still
raking
in
big collections with
the
Williams ‘Four Aces’ novelty piece, released several months back. The novelty item,
we hear, has made quite the sensation
in the
City due to
its close appearance -to a
pinball. Ops are smart enough,
tho,
.not to
refer to the game as such,
in the
City,
but are equally savy
to take advantage
of the unique opportunity
at
their games
locations. Over and above everything,
it’s a great fun game to play and
that’s what
counts in the end.

Halcyon Signs Otis
HOLLYWOOD - Halcyon Manage-
ment has been formed as an off -shoot
of Halcyon Productions. Latter firm,
headed by Harold Cohen, produces the
Johnny Cash Show for ABC-TV and is
also involved with film production.
First client
for the management
firm, which will be run by Michael
Davenport, is Epic's Johnny Otis. The
vet R&B singer/writer/producer has
resumed his career after a long layoff
and is currently drawing critical raves
and heavy crowds to his show at the
Ash Grove in Los Angeles.

Anderson RCA's
LA Field Rep
NEW YORK - Ray Anderson has been
appointed to Los Angeles field promo
rep at RCA Records. Reporting to Dick
Maxwell, sales and promotion manager
for the western region, Anderson is
responsible for radio airplay of RCA
product in the Los Angeles, San Diego,
Phoenix and Honolulu areas, as well
as radio and television promo of artists
when they visit the same region.
For the past year, Anderson handled
promotion for RCA in the Pittsburgh -
Cleveland -Detroit -Buffalo regions. Pre-
viously, Anderson handled local Pitts-
burgh promo for Hamburg Brothers
Distributors. Prior to that, he handled
local promotion for Standard Distribu-
tors in Pittsburgh, where he became
a contributor to the Fenway Reporter,
a national record tip sheet.
GIANT FUNK - That's the largest outdoor advertising board in recording his-
tory, costing some $100,000 (rental space: $70,000; labor and installation: $30,000)
,
just completed on Times Square for Grand Funk Railroad. The name stretches
across the entire length of 45th and 46th (on Broadway) sts. in deep red letters
and bellow are 60 ft. high portraits of the trio. Ad, promoting their new Capitol
album, "Closer To Home," will stand for two months, July and August, accord-
ing to Terry Knight, group's producer and manager, who leased the sign.

Together, Cook and Greenaway started as David and Jonathan a few years back.
Now they are responsible for such hits as the Fortunes "You've Got Your Trou-
bles," Gene Pitney's "Something's Gotten Hold Of My Heart," and Blue Mink's
"Melting Pot" and "Good Morning Freedom." In addition they wrote and produced
the White Plains "My Baby Loves Lovin' " and the follow up "I've Got You On My
Mind." Their own publishing house, Cookaway, handles their compositions as
well as material by other songwriters.
Sue and Sunny, .the pretty songstresses adorning the Brotherhood Of Man,
started out as a group by themselves but got sidetracked by Lesley Duncan (a
songwriter and queen of the British session singers) who persuaded them to go
into session work. Lesley is also responsible for opening the session doors for
Madeline Bell. Madeline came to London with the "Black Nativity" show in 1962,
and met Lesley. Together they backed up Dusty Springfield in all her recordings
for Philips. Later Dusty returned the favor by backing up Madeline for her solo LP.
All in all, the British Hit Factory is a family that looks set to grow into dynastic
proportions. Just the fact that there are so many people of such diverse talents
who have teamed up together, bodes well for the future. While we may not be
hearing from these groups as they are now in years to come, it is quite evident
that all the people involved in this first real musical commune are building a solid
stepping stone towards a bright future.
eric van lustbader

Would you buy a car from this girl? Would you stop jaywalking at this girl's com-
mand? Mavbe you did. Patty Mizzy, secretary to Ed Kaminski (east coast divisional
promotion manager) at Capitol, has held a number of jobs including one of mak-

Age 25, Patty attended private schools

has

Talking a bit more about her work with songwriting, Patty says that the people at
Capitol are expecting her master of the recent foreign she's working on called
"I'm Alive" which she says is kind of like "Those Were The Days." Patty says she
loves her job at the label (this week she brought around the promotion records
because her boss was at the company convention in Hawaii) and tells Ed that
she'll only quit when she has $10,000 in the bank. And, as it looks from here, for
a girl who claims she has had such success simply because she "lucked -out"
every job, that day could be very soon.

HOLLYWOOD (Cont'd from page 37
PUTTING ONES FOOT IN THEIR MOUTH DEPARTMENT: After the foregoing, it
might be nice to take it safe and not talk about records for a week or two, but,
undaunted, we leap right into the fray to praise two recently released albums.
Rhinoceros has made several personnel changes since their second album, and
their third album finds a smaller and differently motivated group. One of the new
additions is drummer Duke Edwards, who shares vocal chores with John Finley.
Edwards, as well as new producer Guy Draper (remember the Unifics?) is very
soul motivated, and that's the way the group is moving now. We haven't seen the
new outfit in action, but the album is definitely their best yet. From friendly
reports filtering thru this office, several major FM'ers are concurring with our own
quality judgement. For all you Danny Weis fans, don't worry, he's still with the
group.
SPECIAL NOTE TO STEVE HARRIS: As Fred Holman said in the New York column
last week, there's a lot to be said for increasing the quality level of pictures avail-
able to the contemporary press. Let Elektra once more lead the way.
SPECIAL NOTE TO ARTIE KORNFELD - The second album we're going to hype is
the first release on your new Eleuthera label by Bert Sommer. In addition to Bert's
major contribution (he is the artist, after all) we'd like to thank you for turning in
your best production ever.
Bert's first album for Capitol, released last year, almost had what it takes, but
just missed the mark. The quality that makes this a better album is that the art-
ist, who's essentially telling of various situations in his own life, has matured and
now has a better perspective on what is going down around him and inside him.
Of course, anybody can sit down and try to describe what he feels and what he
sees. Not everybody can do it very well, and fewer still can describe their life in
such a way that a lot of strangers can identify with them. Bert is one of the few.
When he describes his pain, you can feel it, when he delights in his pleasures, you
find yourself up with him. To make the listeners feel, that is the great art that
Bert Sommer practices very well.
Jefferson Airplane would be the most sought after recording group in the world
right now, if the Rolling Stones were not up for grabs also. Such is life. As life
goes on, the Airplane go on with it, followed by their press agent sending out head-
lines like "Jefferson Airplane Jets To Europe For Bath," which merely tells how
the Airplane will be playing at the famed Bath Festival in Great Britain on June 28,
right after their appearance at the Rotterdam Festival on June 26. Group's PR
chick was nice enough to note that also appearing at Bath will be John Maya'',
Canned Heat, Johnny Winter, Pink Floyd, Fairport Convention, Colosseum, It's A
Beautiful Day, Keef Hartley and, would you believe, the Maynard Ferguson Big
Band, on the first day; while the second day will see the Airplane joined by Led
Zeppelin, the Moody Blues, Steppenwolf, Frank Zappa, the Byrds, the Flock, San-
tana, Dr. John the Night Tripper and Country Joe & the Fish. Thank you Diane.
Jimmy Webb is said to have finally finished his own self -produced album, at an
outrageous cost, after several months of work. LP is up for grabs, but Reprise
is said to have the inside track.
MOVIE STAR DIVISION - Jason Laskay, who was most recently on view in "The
Graduate" (yeah) and is currently making the neighborhood screens in "The
Grasshopper" (thumbs down on that one) has decided to expand his horizons by
entering the record business. He's just been signed to a contract by Art Wayne and
Howard Boggess' new production firm and will start cutting his first sides this
week.
LEFTOVER DEPT. - Because of tight deadlines, we never did print one of the
nicest pictures of the month, which showed Judy Dyble, former lead singer with
Fairport Convention, and Jackie McAuley, former bass player with Them. Duo was
together for the picture because they now have their own little group, Trader
Home, who've issued a pretty little folky album on Janus.
THANK YOU SPACE -A very nice thank you to Stan Moneiro, an old friend who's
now promo head at Metromedia. Stan dropped us a nice line in response to a
recent column on the 50's, of which he was an integral part. Hope to be seeing

Hartman To Address COPME 
cashbox I 
stage 
Modern Jazz Quartet 
RAINBOW GRILL, NYC - The Mod- 
ern Jazz Quartet found itself in what 
even for this group was a slightly un- 
familiar setting when they opened an 
engagement last week at the Rainbow. 
But although the MJQ is not a tradi- 
tional supper club attraction, and de- 
spite the occasional misplacing of a 
fork or spoon during the set, the Quar- 
tet kept the audience intrigued via 
their musical expertise and the sheer 
dynamics of their instrumental inter- 
action. 
The MJQ opened with a few stan- 
dards, "Willow Weep For Me," "It 
Ain't Necessarily So," before doing a 
couple of more contemporary items, 
Tim Hardin's "Misty Roses" and Len- 
non-McCartney's "Yesterday." On the 
last named song, pianist John Lewis 
set down the melody, while vibist Milt 
Jackson overlaid a particularly imag- 
inative improvisational track. 
Turning to some original material, 
the group offered an excerpt from 
Lewis' score for the film, "Kemek," 
which was premiered in its entirety 
during last year's Christmas concert at 
Lincoln Center. Also from the Lewis 
catalog were "The Jasmine Tree," 
"Visitor From Mars," and the even 
more astral "Visitor From Venus." 
These offered Connie Kay the oppor- 
tunity to work with a variety of per- 
cussive instruments and the remark- 
able sounds he produced are probably 
still reverberating lightly somewhere 
in the room. 
The MJQ has been playing together 
for close to two decades now. But 
whereas many groups would have set- 
tled into a comfortable rut, this in- 
credible foursome has shunned the 
easy and obvious, opting instead for 
the adventurous. Both individually and 
collectively they have continued to 
strike out along new jazz routes and 
apparently they plan to continue walk- 
ing point. As well they should. 
e.k. 
The Kinks/Toe Fat 
WHISKY A GO-GO, L.A. - Head Kink 
Ray Davies generously told an enthu- 
siastic audience at a recent Whiskey A 
Go Go outing, "We're not a good group 
and we know it, but we enjoy ourselves 
His statement was half right. The 
Kinks do enjoy themselves and get 
further into it when the people out 
there get turned on to their music and 
performance, as they did at the Whis- 
key. The Kinks are a good group, ac- 
tually two different groups, in effect, 
with different approaches on records 
and in concert, putting out an incred- 
ible amount of energy in both capaci- 
ties. 
I've been a Kinks fan right from the 
beginning, when they unleashed "You 
Really Got Me" and "All Day and All 
of the Night" about five years ago, 
during the first wave of the British in- 
vasion. They epitomized raw rock and 
roll with those tunes and witi the fire 
and appeal of lead singer Davies and 
his cohorts in personal appearances. 
Strangely 
enough, 
they 
never 
achieved complete recognition, even as 
their music got more subtle and com- 
plex, from "Well Respected Gentle- 
man" and "Sunny Afternoon" to the 
recent "Arthur," scored for a televi- 
sion drama and a monumental contri- 
bution to recorded rock. 
The current Kinks include, besides 
Davies, John Dalton on bass, Dave 
Davies playing lead guitar and adding 
vocals, Mick Avory on drums and elec- 
tric piano -organist John Kirksey. On 
wax, most notably with "Arthur," the 
band exhibits an always -changing in- 
ventiveness over a solid, energetic rock 
base, whether using full brass or a sin- 
gle delicate harpischord line. 
On stage the Kinks harken back to 
their early days, still lively, explosive, 
appealing, even lovable, when, for in- 
stance, Ray Davies winks and points 
naughtily at the audience or when 
brother Dave shakes his shaggy locks 
and belts his raucous off-key vocals. 
(A note: Ray Davies has to be one 
of the most exciting singers in pop mu- 
sic. His wobbly, almost drunken deliv- 
ery and his beautifully timed move- 
ments put him up there beside the oft - 
lauded theatrics of Jagger, Morrison 
and Joplin.) 
At their Whiskey gig, the Kinks con- 
centrated on pure energy flow, using 
mostly old material and molding two 
guitars, bass, piano, drums and vocal 
harmonies into 
a 
pulsing electric 
machine. They did a haunting, strong 
"Waterloo Sunset; " "Brainwashed," 
from "Arthur," which equals Kinks in 
its unrelenting drive; the mystical 
"Big Sky," from the "Village Green 
Preservation 
Society" 
album 
and 
ended the set with a "Really Go Me - 
All Day" medley which almost blew 
them off the stage. 
They also fell into a fifties rock jam 
and kicked it all out with Chuck Berry - 
Little Richard licks. Dave Davies' 
playing, while not jaw -dropping, was 
consistently together. 
It might also be noted that drummer 
Avory holds his left hand stick in the 
time-honored manner, cradled in the 
crotch of his thumb and forefinger, 
rather than using it overhand like a 
club, an all too annoying mannerism of 
many rock drummers. And what could 
be heard of Kirksey's keyboard was 
pretty and powerful. 
As a publicity representative said 
later, most of the audience was made 
up of old Kinks fans. "You're either a 
Kinks freak or you're not," she said. 
She's probably right. 
I only caught part of Toe Fat's set. 
That new English group played before 
the Kinks minus their lead singer, who 
blew his voice in earlier sets. What 
was left was an electric blues instru- 
mental trio, adequate but all too famil- 
iar. 
s.s. 
Leon Thomas 
VILLAGE VANGUARD, NYC - When 
Leon Thomas arrives on the stage, you 
get the feeling something good is about 
to take place. Maybe it's the clothes he 
wears, which are beautiful and multi- 
hued. But you think, no, it's the man's 
exuberance, which is evident in his 
shuffling gait and his expression. Then 
he gets to shaking a cowbell, blowing 
a panpipe and throat articulating and 
you forget about the whys as you ex- 
perience the performance of an impor- 
tant new talent. 
During his five day stint at the Van- 
guard, Leon was working with 
a 
smaller group than the one heard on 
his recently released Flying Dutchman 
album. The compactness of the unit 
was well suited to the Vanguard. Off 
the LP came "One" and "Echoes," 
two songs written by the artist, fol- 
lowed by "The Creator Has A Master 
Plan (Peace)," co-authored by Phar- 
aoh Sanders. On this one Leon soon 
had the audience joining in; it spiraled 
upward to a joyful ending. The artist 
also offered an eloquent reading of 
Horace Silver's "Song For My Father." 
Leon deals in a sound which reaches 
into the consciousness of his listeners. 
Using his voice as an instrument and 
weaving his percussive patterns, the 
artist calls up spirits of his ancestors 
and creates an atmosphere which is 
as mental and spiritual as it is musical. 
Not exactly your run of the mill jazz- 
man, Leon Thomas. 
e.k. 
Bass Promoted To 
Chess Exec Producer 
CHICAGO - Ralph Bass has been pro- 
moted from producer at Chess Rec- 
ords to executive producer with the 
label. Bass will now supervise the en- 
tire Chess staff of producers for the 
Chicago -based record complex's Chess, 
Checker, Cadet and Cadet/Concept la- 
bels. 
A producer with Chess for 26 years, 
Bass brought Etta James, Moms Mab- 
ley, Pigmeat Markham and Mitty Col- 
lier to the label. 
Before joining Chess, Bass produced 
for Black and White, Savoy and King 
Records. He produced James Brown's 
"Please, Please, Please" for King as 
well as Earl Bostic's instrumentals for 
that label. Records by the Dominoes 
and the Royals on King were also pro- 
duced by Bass. ("Open The Door Rich- 
ard" by Jack McVey was his first hit 
production.) 
Other major R&B acts that Bass 
has produced are T -Bone Walker, 
Hank Ballard and the Midnighters, 
Johnny Otis and Winonie Harris. With 
Chess, Bass has worked in jazz as well 
as R&B, producing records by such 
artists as Ramsey Lewis.

Composer Tobias Dies 
NEW YORK - Charles Tobias, com- 
poser, author and music publisher- 
died in New York at the age of 72. He 
was the writer of such songs as "Miss 
You", "When Your Hair Has Turned 
To Silver", "Don't Sit Under The 
Apple Tree" and "Those Lazy Hazy 
Crazy Days of Summer".

NEW YORK - SHORT TAKES BY THE NUMBER, SHORT ACHES BY THE SCORE 
Last week's column was all short takes. Because of the large number of them 
left over, though, we'll print another lot of them heavily interdíspersed with some 
first-hand bits (including a Cannonball Adderley interview). Read on, read on. 
Blood, Sweat & Tears was more than just the name of a band the other day in 
Bucharest, Rumania. It was also a pretty fair description of the proceedings as the 
Columbia group gave a performance which wound up in a virtual riot. Apparently, 
the Bucharest police aren't used to what has become the standard audience par- 
ticipation closer for rock concerts in the Western world. When enthusiastic fans 
attempted to storm the stage, the cops reacted by wading into them with flying 
clubs. When the smoke cleared, a number of young people had been injured and 
ít was announced that the remainder of the band's State Department sponsored 
tour had been cancelled. BS&T had planned to do an additional concert in Ploesti. 
Other news of the week ís of the Newport Jazz Festival on July 10 to 12. Set to 
go on Saturday is Ike And Tina Turner and, ín celebration of his birthday, Bill 
Cosby will present his group, Badfoot Brown and The Bunions Bradford Marching 
and Funeral Band. Also on tap for their predominantly blues performances are 
Roberta Flack, Albert King and Shuggie Otis. All are "first -timers" at the festival 
who will take their place among a full slate of top jazzmen. 
About the Cosby band: Uni ís going to release the group's first album this week 
on which the actor/comedían performs on a number of instruments and com- 
poses all the music. Produced by Gil Rodin, the set features Cos in a serious vein. 
Still on a jazz note, Warner's Herbie Hancock is heading up a group of show 
business people to build a Harlem Jazz Center in that community. The pianist/ 
composer wants to start the center to provide professionals and students of the 
Arts with the opportunities to research, create and present their work to the public. 
Julian "Cannonball" Adderley just visited us to talk about his black music semi- 
nar program and his upcoming Capitol release. The LP will include the group 
playing with a symphony orchestra. Three major pieces will be presented: one by 
his producer, David Axelrod; another by Lalo Schifrin; and the Viennese composer 
Jawinul penned a work that takes 22 minutes of album time. The album gets into 
a lot of free -form stuff into which is worked all types of music - rock, R&B, bal- 
lads, old swing, and styles of Archie Shepp, Ornette Coleman, Don Ellis, etc. 
Cannonball comments on his change of direction on this LP in the following way: 
"Music has so many characteristics and the band can play anything very well. 
(Con't. on Page 40) 
HOLLYWOOD - THEY SHOO-IN HORSES, DON'T THEY? 
Songsmiths maintain that their most gratifying experience ís to come across 
kids in the street who are humming, whistling or singing their compositions. We 
agree. Back ín the fifties, when we were adding words to music, we would con- 
stantly encounter saplings singing our songs and ít never ceased to amaze and 
enchant us - even though they were our kids. 
It was a dozen years ago when we wrote our one and only horse -race song. 
It began "Well, 
I bet my bottom dollar on a nag called Sarah Rose/In the fifth at 
Caliente/Fifty dollars on the nose/On our parimutual ticket she was 95 to 1/And 
I 
wondered why the odds were high/then 
I saw her run ... 'They're off,' the grand- 
stand shouted/As they started in to race/Sarah Rose took off like 'Lightning'/ 
'Lightning' was ín 14th place/As they headed for the backstretch/In a final burst 
of speed/01' Sarah Rose, by just a nose/Was a mile behind the lead ... " It was 
titled "Monkey on a Donkey" and íf you consider the first two of thirty-four verses 
as undeserving, we'll hum a few bars. 
We showed them to a number of music biz people and, almost without excep- 
tion, they took exception to one word in the song. "You're on the wrong track," 
they said, "there are no parimutuals at Caliente." We had no idea how knowledge- 
able our trade was - about horse racing. 
Since, we have discovered that a great many industry execs and artists escape 
from the weekday record rat race to a weekend Hollypark horse race. And the 
list of horse racing owners ín this biz is impressive and prodigious. It includes 
(and we're sure this ís only a partial list) exec -producers Snuff Garrett, Ken Rever - 
comb, Joe Saracino; D.J. Bob Hudson; music pubs and producers Sy Heller, 
Ray Harris, Bill Lowery; execs Jerry Moss, Russ Regan, Herb Alpert; pressing 
plant proprietor Nate DuRoff; record promoman Mike Borchetta; songsmíth-con- 
ductor-producer Burt Bacharach; former label prexy (in the process, we hear, of 
forming his own new label) Alvin Bennett and vocalist Tommy Roe. 
A couple of years back, at the NARM convention, Bacharach abashedly excused 
himself from a panel discussion, explaining that he had to leave a little early be- 
cause he had his first horse racing at Del Mar. Since Burt has seldom done wrong 
with a song, half of NARM figured his nag was a sure thing. And many wandered 
out of the auditorium to contact their local bookies, laying a sawbuck or two on 
Bacharach's entry. From the flick and disk trades Bacharach gets Oscars and 
Grammys. But from his horses - mostly promises, promises. 
He owns six at the moment, including one that recently ran in the San Juan 
Capistrano Handicap. "I'm planning to spend this summer at Del Mar," Burt re- 
cently told L.A. Times nightclub editor Bob Hilburn, "we've rented a house right 
on the beach ... racing is the only thing that lets me forget music completely." 
Snuff Garrett ís one of very few ín our trade who is actually ahead of the game 
with his stable. In the past few months Snuff has had more horses than records 
ín the top three. His trainer, George Hartstone (former president of Hart Distrib- 
utors) insists that Garrett is simply enjoying beginner's luck. "Hardly anybody 
ever makes money racing horses," says Hartstone. "That's why it's the sport of 
Kings." George also trains the Jerry Moss, Nate DuRoff, Al Bennett and Herb 
Alpert stables. 
Mike Borchetta, involved ín split ownership with Bill Lowery and Bob Hudson, 
contends that he ís turning a neat profit on his weekend venture. "But that's only 
because 
I also board horses." Still Borchetta's colors have reached the winner's 
circles on numerous occasions - three times this year. 
Tommy Roe, we're told, recently coughed up ten grand for a horse - a yearling 
(Con't. on Page 40) 
John Hammond/Fran McKendree of McKendree Spring 
Jerry Jeff Walker/Cannonball Adderley

Blue Thumb Readies 
2nd `Color Collage' LP 
LOS ANGELES - Having introduced 
its "Stereo Color Collage' multi -hued 
record with Dave Mason's album, 
"Alone Together," Blue Thumb Rec- 
ords next "Color Collage" LP will be 
"Buddy And The Juniors." This al- 
bum will be released in August. 
"Buddy And The Juniors" is the 
first time teaming of Buddy Guy, 
Junior Wells and Junior Mance. The 
project was conceived by Philadel- 
phia disk jockey Michael Cuscuna of 
WMMR-FM and financed by Blue 
Thumb. 
The colors used in this package 
differ significantly from those used 
on the Mason LP which is now Blue 
Thumb's top selling and fastest mov- 
ing album. Various grades of black 
and white are blended into the blues 
album, which features all accoustic 
instruments and no drums. 
The repertoire performed by ran- 
ges from "Talkin' Bout Women Ob- 
viously" to "Riffin," "Buddy's Blues," 
"Hoochie Coochie Man," "Five Long 
Years," "Rock Me Mama" and "Ain't 
No Need." 
Creedence Gold Album 
Heads Fantasy Release 
OAKLAND - "Cosmo's Factory," the 
new 
LP by Creedence Clearwater 
Revival-fifth in the series of LPs by 
Creedence-is a Gold Album as of 
the moment of release. Advance or- 
ders on the LP, which was released 
July 8, totaled over $1 million. 
The new Creedence LP contains 
seven original compositions by John 
Fogerty, lead singer and guitarist. 
Four of the songs in the LP have pre- 
viously been out on singles: "Up 
Around the Bend," "Run Through the 
Jungle," 
"Travelin' 
Band" 
and 
"Who'll Stop the Rain." Three of the 
songs are new. Fogerty produced the 
album. 
Included in the material on the LP 
is a Fogerty arrangement of "My 
Baby Left Me," a composition of vet- 
eran blues singer Arthur "Big Boys' 
Crudup, "Before You Accuse Me," 
one of Bo Diddley's hits, and "I 
Heard It Through The Grape Vine," 
standard. 
Also on the Fantasy July release 
schedule are two other new LPs, one 
by Billie Joe Becoat, "Let's Talk for 
Awhile" and "Parish Hall." 
Becoat's LP is his second for Fan- 
tasy (his first was released in 1969) . 
It was produced by Jesse Osborne. 
Parish Hall is a new group making its 
first recording debut with the Fantasy 
LP.

NEW YORK - Jazz artist Joe Farrell 
has been signed to an exclusive con- 
tract by CTI Records. He is now re- 
cording his first album for the label, 
set for an August release. Farrell 
won the 1970 Down Beat readers poll 
as top soprano sax player.

Pop Picks 
HELLO DARLIN' - Conway Twitty - Decca 
DL 75209 
Another country artist crosses the border into 
pop territory. Actually, Conway Twitty's done it 
before, but not in a while, and it was a surprise 
to find his single, "Hello, Darlin'," on the Top 
100. Now the album of the same name has hit 
the Top 100 Albums chart. Twitty is obviously 
an artist to be watched closely. His career may 
take some sudden turns. 
BLACK TALK! - Charles Earland - Prestige 
7758 
Jazz organist Charles Earland has come out 
of nowhere onto the charts. Assisted by Virgil 
Jones, trumpet; Houston Person, tenor sax; Mel- 
vin Sparks, guitar; Idris Muhammed, drums; 
and Buddy Caldwell, conga, Earland has made 
an album that has a wider appeal than any jazz 
organ set we can remember. LP has five selec- 
tions, including "Aquarius," "More Today Than 
Yesterday" (just released as a single) and the 
title tune. Watch this one closely for further ac- 
tion.

Pop Best Bets 
GREAT EXPECTATIONS - Kiki Dee - Tamla 
TS303 
Take one established British session singer, 
add an excellent record company that knows 
what it's about, sprinkle in arrangers and mu- 
sicians of style and taste building on rock solid 
songs and you have some idea of what this 
premier LP from Kiki Dee is like. But not quite. 
Here's a girl with one of the finest new voices 
around who has been struggling for some time 
in England with the wrong material. Suddenly, 
as happened when Dusty Springfield moved 
to Atlantic, Kiki's voice is finally liberated. Best 
cuts include "I Can't Give Back The Love and 
the moving "Jimmy."

Jazz Picks 
THE SIXTH SENSE - Lee Morgan --Blue Note 
BST 84335 
Lee Morgan, who as a teenager was already 
playing to acclaim in Dizzy Gillespie's band, 
has continued to seek out fresh musical direc- 
tions. The trumpet player adds another chapter 
to his story with an album which never lags 
in intensity of feeling and musical spirit. Though 
Morgan's presence is everywhere, the talents 
of his comrades in sound, four of whom are 
alumni of Art Blakey groups, contribute consid- 
erably to the LP's overall sound. Solid jazz entry. 
A DAY IN COPENHAGEN - Dexter Gordon - 
Prestige 7763 
Tenor sax man Dexter Gordon assembled a 
uniquely talented group of expatriate jazz musi- 
cians and they have come up with an album 
which is as refreshing as its title. Three Slide 
Hampton originals highlight a set which also in- 
cludes the contemporary standard, "The Shadow 
Of .Your Smile." Slide is heard on trombone and 
Kenny Drew offers some neat piano work. Gordon 
himself is in characteristically fine form on this 
worthwhile LP.

English Language Dominates
Almost 50%
of
all pop records
re-
leased in Europe are in English, with
35%
the
probable
figure
for
South
America and other countries. In Ger-
many, probably due to the Air Force
Network
and
the
Voice
of
America
broadcast,
this
figure was quoted
as
75
to 80%.
In Sweden
and Belgium
writers are attempting lyrics in Eng-
lish
in
an
effort
to
improve
the
saleability of their songs.
'The imme-
diate
result
of
all
this
is
talk
of
national
quotas
such
as
that which
Canada
is attempting;
but
the
con-
census
of
opinion, backed by
experi-
ence in Brazil and other countries,
is
that
these
will
fail
because
if
the
public can’t get the music
it wants on
native
stations, they
will tune
in on
foreign
stations. The impact
of
this
on local sponsors has caused the quo-
tas, in some cases, to be dropped.

real thing.” Many of the show’s songs have a solid-
ly commercial
flair, and they are being picked up by numerous singers and groups
(The Sweet
Inspiration was one
of the
first to wax two
of the songs from
the
show on
Atlantic, and their reading, along with the back-up of the Muscle Shoals
sidemen— is
hit sound).
All
in
all, from the time the idea was conceived
until the
time of final rehearsals, took only about a year.
Before "Nobody,” Gary worked as a teacher
in Bedford Stuyvesant and picked
up extra bread doing pop TV and
radio commercials. He’s also written
a "Rock
Oratorio” which he describes as "a contemporary Hebrew thing, done by re-setting
the whole Friday night service to today music.”
It’s been done several times locally
and
is set to tour nationwide.
Right now, Gary's working on a "Broadway dimen-
sion”
musical
that
will
have
“subtle,
political
undercurrents,
similar
to
those
utilized by various
classical composers.” Remember the man’s name— it will be
most familiar
in composer circles for some time to come.
OUT OF THE HOME AND INTO THE FRYING PAN
The music of Don Cooper young Roulette folk artist
is filled with
recollections.
Recollections of places, aspirations, women. His songs most of which he’s written
tell more about where he’s been than where he’s at exuding moods of loneliness
and an attempt to relate past recollections to present experiences.
It should come as no surprise then
that the 23-year-old
artist has been
con-
stantly on the move
primarily
in the Midwest where he’s witnessed countless
life
styles and developed an
understanding
of the area’s people—an
understanding
that has been sensitively transferred to his songs.
Among the places Don has called home are Kansas City,
St.
Paul, Des Moines
and
Columbia,
Missouri, where
he attended
the
University of Missouri
for four
years, receiving a degree
in
English Educaton.
He considers Columbia home now because, he says, he’s never stayed anywhere
more than four years.
“I don’t recall a home,” Don says, "and
I guess traveling so
much has
left me with
a
lot of disassociated feelings.”
In
his conversation and
in music, Don does not condemn or apologize for his
wanderlust.
Rather,
he
appreciates
his
travels
for
contributing
to
an
in-depth
understanding of diverse
life styles and
a
rich realm of experiences.
Don
is
still traveling,
but
his
itinerary has become more structured.
It now
in-
cludes the Powder Ridge
Festival, the Merv Griffin Show, and studio work toward
a
third
Roulette album,
a follow-up to
his “Bless the Children”
LP.
Don’s goals are simply stated but ambitious.
"I want to make good music the
rest of my
life,” he says. Don’s efforts thus far in a
brief career indicate that
his
goals are
achievable.
But just where, geographically,
that music
will be made
is
anybody’s guess.

HE'S STILL A MYSTERY—The
identity
of our Mystery Man
cyclist has gone un-
guessed
for
a
precedent shattering second week. The rumor that he
is actually
one
of Morty Wax’s clients has proved to be unfounded.
On Saturday morning,
the Mystery Man pulled up stake (he only had one) and took to the back roads of
America.
His destination, Los Angeles.
After a day of pedaling on
his trusty ten
speed, he managed to get to Nyack,
N.Y., a rather disappointing accomplishment,
even
by
his own admission.
After
all,
there
are
people who commute that
far
every
morning.
But the MM had some good
excuses
for
his
poor showing:
his
pack had begun
spilling gear
all over the road,
plus he had taken several wrong
turns and narrowly escaped a rock slide on the Palisades.
Determined to stick to
his
quest,
he
rose
early the
next
day,
cycled
to
a
point 1,284
feet above sea
level (the highest he’s been
in several months) and coasted down four miles into
the Delaware
River Valley where he made camp
in
a cemetery.
Despite
a soggy
duffelbag (he’d accidentally flooded
it with
root beer), he was
in good shape and
good
spirits at last report.
Once again we pose the question, Who
is the Mystery
Man?
Hint:
he’s
in the record business,
in fact you might say he’s kicked around
it.
First
answer
(correct)
wins
the
Dolly
Holiday
album.
More
clues
in
next
week's column.

Key radio stations throughout the

second spots featuring various cuts 
from the Komix album,

rotic Reaction," and "Little Little."

newspapers,

aminer. Los Angeles Times, Boston 
Globe, Baltimore Sun, Miami Herald, 
Chicago Tribune, New York Post, 
Detroit News, New Haven Journal, 
Philadelphia Daily News, Philadelphia 
Bulletin, among others. Undergrounds 
include: Fusion, Rolling Stone, Bos- 
ton After Dark, Great Speckled Bird, 
Chicago Seed, Zygote, Village Voice, 
Creem, Distant Drummer. 
Radio spots are being run on such 
maior stations as, 
WBCN-Boston, 
KFRC-San Francisco, WOR-FM-New 
Kaye To Farrell 
In Writing Pact 
NEW YORK-Wes Farrell Organ- 
ization has signed exclusive contracts 
with Thomas Kaye as a writer to his 
Pocket Full Of Tunes publishing com- 
pany. Farrell, together with Charlie 
Brown, will also produce Kaye's first 
album as an artist. 
Among Kaye's most notable produc- 
tion credits are hits for Maxine 
Brown, 
the 
Shirelles, and 
Chuck 
Jackson, including the million -seller 
single "Hold On I'm Coming," by 
Chuck Jackson and Maxine Brown. 
During the past year, he produced 
two hits for Jay and the Americans, 
"This Magic Moment," and "Walkin' 
In The Rain." In addition, he has 
completed album products soon to be 
released with such artists as Gene 
McDaniels, Freddy Scott and The 
Exciters and is currently completing 
an album with Wilbert Harrison which 
is being recorded live at the Canaan 
Baptist Church in Harlem and is 
backed with a 160 voice choir. 
Kaye has also written "Thanks For 
Nothin' " for the television documen- 
tary "Black News." In the past six 
weeks, many artists have recorded 
"Thanks For Nothin'." Kaye is pro- 
viding all the music for that docu- 
mentary as well as the soundtrack for 
another ABC-TV documentary 
on 
drugs scheduled for this fall. 
York, 
WFIL-Philadelphia, WDAS-

Tom Kennedy, director of advertis- 
ing and marketing for Colussus, is 
supervising the market by market ad 
and marketing activities relating to 
the LP, which include: direct coopera- 
tion and communication with all dis- 
tributors, utilizing posters, window 
streamers, and counter displays for

Vance To Compose 
Pinkville' Score 
NEW YORK-Singer-composer Joel 
Vance has been named to compose 
the music and lyrics for the play 
"Pinkville" and will appear in the 
production with his group, Big City, 
at the Berkshire Theatre in Stock- 
bridge, Mass. from August 13 to 18, 
prior to a Broadway opening in the 
fall. 
"Pinkville," which deals with vio- 
lence as exemplified by the My Lai 
massacre, was written by George Ta- 
bors, author of "Brecht On Brecht," 
produced by Lyn Austin, who recently 
produced "Indians" starring Stacy 
Keach on Broadway, and directed by 
Grover Dale.

CBS Talent Roster Highlights 
Sales Convention In Freeport 
FREEPORT, BAHAMAS-The pre- 
sentation of local foreign recordings 
formed one of the high points of CBS 
International's 
Freeport, 
Bahamas 
meetings last week. CBS subsidiaries 
from various parts of the world show- 
cased samples of their newest pop 
and classical product for other CBS 
International Convention delegates as 
well as for Columbia Records person- 
nel. 
The A&R presentations came at the 
end of two days of general business 
meetings. These were attended by 54 
CBS 
International 
representatives 
from the New York headquarters, 
and from overseas operational offices 
and local subsidiaries. 
Latin America 
From Latin America, both CBS Ar- 
gentina and CBS Mexico served up 
samples of the latest kinds of music 
happening to the south of the U. S. 
Argentina presented records by the 
artists who currently are on the local 
charts: 
Sandro, 
Leonardo 
Favio, 
Piero, Los Naufragos, and Fedra y 
Maximiliano. At the same time, they 
introduced two new young talents: 
the Cuarteto Zupay and Estela Ra- 
val. Mexico utilized film, slides and 
tapes 
to introduce the 
music of 
Vicente 
Fernandes, 
Sonora 
San- 
tanera, Las Ventanas, Mario y su De- 
safinado 4, and Los Piccolinos. 
CBS France 
A number of European subsidiaries 
demonstrated that their A&R staffs 
have, in a relatively short time, es- 
tablished a number of strong artists 
and, at the same time, developed new 
talent. CBS France showcased French 
language 
recordings 
by 
Marie 
Laforet, Les Irresistibles, Michel Fu - 
gain, Les Albatros, Jean-Jacques De- 
bout, Danyel Gerard, Annie Cordy, 
and Charles Trenet; and instrumen- 
tals by ,Caravelli and Manitas de Pla- 
ta. The international quality of CBS 
France's product was emphasized by 
the recordings of Joe Dassin 
(in 
French, German, Italian 
and En- 
glish), Pilar Thomas (in French and 
Spanish), Zizi Jeanmaire (in Spanish 
and German), Les Compagnons de la 
Chanson (in French, Japanese and 
German) and Titanic (in English). 
The French company also introduced 
a new recording of choir music by 
the Spandauer Kantorei of Berlin. 
Germany 
CBS Germany emphasized the clas- 
sics with exerpts from Ivan Rebroff's 
latest recordings, highlighted by a 
film of Rebroff doing "The Death of 
Boris 
Goudonov." 
Germany 
also 
showed its classical strength with 
new product by the celebrated Ger- 
man tenor, Rene Kollo, as well as a 
new LP by pianist, Nelson Freire. 
Pert songstress, Mary Roos, exem- 
plified German pop sounds of today. 
Italy & Holland 
From Italy, a 16mm. film featuring 
leading top -sellers such as Massimo 
Ranieri, Renato dei Profeti, and 
'I 
Cameleonti was shown. Also high- 
lighted on film were new iItalian ar- 
tist Gianni Nazzaro, Orlando & Pis - 
tocchi, and Nieman, a sensational 
young singer from Poland, now liv- 
ing in Italy. 
From Holland, CBS-Artone pre- 
sented new LP's by jazz pianist 
Louis Van Dyke and vocalist Chris 
Hinze. 
England 
CBS England unveiled new rec- 
ordings by some of their top -selling 
acts including Christie, whose first 
single, "Yellow River," made number 
one in Great Britain; the Tremeloes; 
and Georgie Fame. A sampling of 
new British contemporary talent was 
also presented. On the classical side, 
Cash Box - August 8, 1970 
a new recording of Debussy's "Pel- 
leas," conducted by Pierre. Boulez, 
was introduced. Other new Boulez 
LP's as well 
as 
one 
by pianist 
Charles Rosen were highlighted. 
Japan 
CBS 
SONY of Japan conducted 
viewers on a two-year retrospective, 
recapping the building of a roster of 
local popular and classical artists 
that, today, numbers more than 30. 
Canada 
Columbia Records of Canada pre- 
viewed new material which indicated 
that music from that country will 
continue to have a strong influence 
on the U. S. charts. Among the ar- 
tists presented were Alan J. Ryan, 
the Perth Country Conspiracy, and 
Mashmakhan. 
Rebroff Appears 
CBS International also invited ev- 
eryone attending the Columbia Rec- 
ords national sales convention to 
meet Ivan Rebroff at a poolside cock- 
tail reception last Sat. 
Film Music Upsurge In Japan; King 
Offers `Definitive' 7 -LP Package 
HOLLYWOOD - Japan is the most 
rapidly growing record market in the 
world. 'It should soon be second to 
the U. S., topping even Great Bri- 
tain's burgeoning sales. This, 
ac- 
cording to Ron Eyre, deputy director 
of Liberty-U.A.'s International divi- 
sion and Patrick Boyle, L. A. office 
International manager for the labels, 
can be directly attributed to that na- 
tion's fascination for and tremendous 
interest in the western way of life. 
"Baseball was probably the first 
indication 
of that interest," says 
Eyre. But our western flicks started 
to catch on in the 50's. It now encom- 
passes a variety of western cultures. 
And particularly classical, jazz and 
motion picture music." 
"Japan probably does more with a 
movie soundtrack album than any 
country outside the U. S., occasional- 
ly outstripping the states," 
says 
Boyle. He points to "Battle of Bri- 
tain" as an example. The soundtrack 
LP outsold both Britain and the U. 
S. "Man and a Woman" topped the 
Eurovision Contest Revisions 
Aim At Reviving Fest Interest 
LONDON - Major changes will be 
made in the organization of next 
year's Eurovision Song Contest to be 
held April 3rd at the Gaiety Theater, 
Dublin. 
Staging the event at an estimated 
cost of £10,000 will be Radio Telefis 
Eireann, and the different set-up is 
being introduced 
to overcome the 
controversies and disagreements of 
past Eurovision tournys which have 
caused several countries to drop out 
and also revive a waning public in- 
terest in the event. The 1971 juries 
will consist of two members only 
from each country instead of the ten 
used hitherto. One juror must be un- 
der 25 years old, and the other above 
that age level, but none will be per- 
mitted under 18 or over 60. Each 
juror will have five votes and will 
award each song in points out of five 
and for the first time in the contest's 
history, the juries will attend the 
event instead of voting by radio tele- 
phone. Their travelling expenses will 
be paid by the countries they rep- 
resent but this will be the only pay- 
ment they will receive. 
Public Exposure 
The public will be able to hear all 
the contesting songs before the actu- 
al vocal joust takes place by means 
of telerecordings made by the partici- 
pants. 
Nimbus 9/RCA Productions Increase 
TORONTO - Nimbus 
9 and RCA 
have been working so closely togeth- 
er it's only natural they are being 
regarded as a team of one. 
Jack Richardson, one of the princi- 
ples of Nimbus 9 and producer of the 
Guess Who, has been cranking out 
productions under both labels. His 
anchor group, The Guess Who from 
Winnipeg, are now making the big 
chart noise with their recent release, 
"Hand Me Down World." On the do- 
mestic front RCA has just released a 
couple of Bill Misener productions 
that could shake the recording scene. 
The disk having the most potential 
would appear to be ".I Don't Believe" 
by Vancouver's Canada. The plug 
side was written by group organist 
Clyde Harvey. Formerly Fox, this 
group have found an eager following 
throughout Upper Canada and are 
currently on a tour of the Western 
Provinces. The disc has already been 
picked up by radio stations in the 
areas in which they are known. 
Also a big plus for Misener is his 
production of "In 
The Rain" by 
Tranquillity Base, a strong follow-up 
to their "If You're Lookin"' deck. An 
interesting switch was the RCA To- 
ronto studios' recording session by 
Montreal's French Revolution. Out of 
this has come "The Dawn Of The 
Revolution" with the orchestration 
and arrangements by Misener. Otta- 
wa's Marshmallow Group have also 
come up with a Misner production in 
"Sing To 
My Lover" written by 
group member Tim Eaton and their 
manager Vern Craig. Misener is a 
producer for RCA's Sun -Bar Produc- 
tions.

7 LP's, 84 Songs 
This week, King Records, U.A.'s 
licensee in the Orient, will be releas- 
ing what Eyre terms is the "defini- 
tive" collection of film themes, It will 
certainly be the most ambitious al- 
bum set in the history of soundtrack 
and film music, including 84 songs on 
seven 
LP's, handsomely packaged 
with a 100 page four-color hard cov- 
er book -brochure. Set, titled "Gala 
Collection of Screen Music," includes 
three U. A. LP's featuring the music 
of Leroy Holmes, two Seven Seas 
and two London disks. 
A similar 
package of five additional LP's is 
currently in preparation. Eyre says 
there are no plans to release the 
same product in the U. S., since dup- 
lication here would 
be financially 
prohibitive. 
The project was undertaken as a 
result of what Eyre terms Japan's 
"total involvement" in film songs. 
Double album sets like U. A.'s film 
themes to the James Bond features 
average 
between 
25-30 
thousand 
units. "There is a much closer liason 
between film distribs and record firms 
in Japan than here," says Eyre, "ad- 
ding to the escalation of film album 
project sales." 
Jazz Sells, Too 
Boyle adds that U. A. -Liberty -Blue 
Note jazz acts such as Jimmy Smith 
and Ornette Coleman are enormous 
record names in Japan. 
Boyle & Eyre 
Brit. At MIDEM: 
Bd Of Trade Sets 
Lower Subsidy 
LONDON - The Board of Trade 
subsidy for British partipants in the 
1971 MIDEM meet has been reduced 
by approximately 150. The primary 
reason is that the Board has to sup- 
port other industries in a similar 
fashion and the £50,000 it spent on 
the 1970 MIDEM was the second 
highest total it has ever invested 
in a trade fair. Smaller companies 
prepared to share office accommoda- 
tion in pairs will still be able to 
attend without 
cash outlay. 
The 
equivalent of two entire floors of the 
Palais des Festivals at Cannes has 
already been booked by disk and pub- 
lishing companies from all over the 
world including 35 British firms.

Moody Blues 
Cop 1st Gold 
NEW YORK - The Moody Blues 
have been certified for their first gold 
album. Certification was confirmed 
this week by the Record Industry As- 
sociation of America (RIAA) for to 
"Our Children's Children's Children," 
on the Moody Blues' own Threshold 
label, nationally distributed by Lon- 
don Records. Gold records will be 
awarded to Justin Hayward, Graeme 
Edge, Mike Pinder, Ray Thomas, 
John Lodge and their producer, Tony 
Clarke. 
Previous Moody Blues material ap- 
peared on Deram Records. Several of 
the group's earlier LP's are now clos- 
ing in on the gold record level of 
$1,000.000 in sales with certification 
possible within the next 
several 
weeks. 
Meanwhile, the group is now ex- 
pected back in the United States for 
a brief tour. Anticipated dates await- 
ing confirmation from London are 
September 17 to 27, during which the 
group will be working every night in 
a different city. Tour is being set by 
CMA. 
Blues 'Rides' Gold 
NEW YORK - The Blues Image 
have earned their first gold record 
when their Atco single, "Ride Cap- 
tain Ride" certified as a million seller 
by the Record Industry Association 
of America (RIAA). "Ride" was tak- 
en from the Blues Image second al- 
bum on Atco, "Open," which was is- 
sued last Jan. It was released as a 
single after it broke out of the LP. 
The Blues Image, now on a nation- 
al tour, will make their first appear- 
ance at the Fillmore East later this 
month (21 & 22). 
Plumb Single Has 
An Intl Flavor 
LOS ANGELES - Producer Neely 
Plumb has created an "international" 
single combining an Italian melody, 
English language lyrics, British in- 
strumentalists, Italian chorus and an 
American lead singer. 
The single is "The Fortune Cookie 
Song" which IMC Productions, for 
whom Plumb works, will place with a 
record company for distribution. 
The song was written in Italy, ac- 
cording to Plumb and became a hit in 
Japan several months ago as sung by 
a young girl. Plumb received exclu- 
sive rights from its publisher, Peer 
Southern, to create a record for the 
U. S. market. While in London sever- 
al months ago, Plumb had a lyric 
written and cut the orchestral track 
with 26 pieces conducted by Nicky 
Welsh. 
From London, he went to Rome on 
business and located a children's 
chorus to sing an Italian refrain 
which runs through the song. That 
was added onto the tracks in Rome. 
Then when he returned to Los Ange- 
les, 
he 
recorded his 
12 -year 
old 
daughter Eve, as the lead voice.

Due to the unprecedented growth

Reprise Readies 
Hendrix -Redding LP 
BURBANK - An album of per- 
formances by Otis Redding and the 
Jimi Hendrix Experience at the Mon- 
terey International Pop Festival is 
being prepared for mid -August re- 
lease by Reprise Records. 
Producer Lou Adler gave the com- 
pany rights to the performances un- 
der an agreement negotiated by Mo 
Ostin, president of Warner 
Bros. 
Records. Lou Adler and John Phillips 
produced the festival and the album, 
which is titled, "Otis Redding/The 
Jimi 
Hendrix 
Experience/Historic 
Performances Recorded at the Mon- 
terey Pop Festival." 
Parts of the Monterey tapes were 
used for the soundtrack of "Monterey 
Pop," a documentary film of the 
event, but none of the musical mate- 
rial from the festival has previously 
been available on records. 
Otis Redding's performance on the 
record includes his in -person versions 
of "Shake," "Respect," "I've Been 
Loving You Too Long," "Satisfac- 
tion" and "Try a Little Tenderness." 
The Jimi Hendrix Experience is 
captured in its first United States 
appearance, a show which included 
"Like a Rolling Stone," "Rock Me, 
Baby," "Can You See Me" and "Wild 
Thing"-the latter song a seven - 
minute version which 
ended with 
Hendrix setting fire to his guitar. 
Warner Bros. plans a large-scale 
advertising, 
promotion 
and 
sales 
campaign to accompany the release 
of the album, according 
to Stan 
Cornyn, the company's director of 
creative services. 
Cornyn said the campaign, which 
includes extensive radio and print ad- 
vertising and special merchandising 
aids, is one of the largest in the 
history of the company. 
B.B. King, Mgr. 
Open Prod. Co. 
NEW YORK - B. B. King, ABC/ 
Dunhill recording artist has formed 
a 
record 
production 
company 
in 
partnership with his manager, Sid- 
ney A. Seidenberg. First act signed 
by the company is a two -man blues 
group, Malcolm and Chris, both 19 
years old. It is also the first act, since 
B. B. King himself, to be added to 
Seidenberg's artist management firm, 
Sidney A. Seidenberg, Inc. 
In managing Malcolm and Chris 
Seidenberg will use the same formula 
that has proved successful with B. B. 
King. This includes, Seidenberg says, 
heavy promotion and publicity aimed 
at the youth market. 
Malcolm and Chris were discovered 
last year in Dayton, Ohio by B. B. 
King while he was playing an en- 
gagement there. Their first LP, "Just 
The Blues," is scheduled for release 
in early August, on the BluesTime 
label.

cording 
to

Johnson. 
"Studio One fills Chicago's increasing

Hendrix Launches 
Electric Lady 
NEW YORK - Super star Jimi Hen- 
drix has arrived in New York in anti- 
cipation of the August 26 opening of 
his recording studio, Electric Lady at 
52 West Eighth Street. Electric Lady 
contains two studios, the larger of 
which has 36 tracks and is acoustical- 
ly divided into a live and dead side of 
the room. Other facilities 
of the 
studio include colored lights, a moog 
synthesizer, and a plush decor which 
is consistent with the Hendrix image. 
The studio was designed by Eddy 
Kramer, chief engineer. Maintenance 
Engineer is Shimon Ron and Kim 
King is the second engineer. Jon 
Storyk was the architect of the 
studio which is managed by Jim Mar- 
ron. Electric Lady has already been 
used by several artists including Buzz 
Linhart Elliot Randall, Irene Reid, 
Glory River, Hendrix himself and 
Led Zeppelin, who mixed their latest 
LP there.

NEW YORK-ALMOST FREE SAMPLES 
Where do you turn when you realize you're listening to records that are forty 
minutes of a heavy group trying to scare you to death with their mean, minor 
key music; or a band that is swinging along just too softly; or a soloist whose 
voice gets grating after the seventh cut? One place to turn is to sampler records 
or sampler -type records. There is a big difference between the two. On one hand 
there are the samplers that can be purchased only through the mail, and then 
there are the ones that are commercial, record store albums. Both contain 
selections by different artists from the sampler's label or from different label 
affiliations. 
By far, the leader in the non-commercial field is Warner/Reprise who has 
four samplers amazingly priced at $2, a new one titled "Alternatives" at $1, 
and another sampler put together by Frank Zappa called "Zapped" which is also 
priced at one buck. All are mail-order, and all but the last two are double 
record sets. The albums feature most of the labels' artists with the majority of 
cuts coming from the performer's LP's as well as some first -time -released cuts 
(like Jimi Hendrix' "Stone Free" from the "Record Show" sampler). One of the 
better features of their packages is extensive bio and incidental notes on each 
of the artists featured in the sets. 
The commercial samplers are interesting, too. My favorites are the two from 
MGM-both film soundtrack albums: "Zabriske Point" and "The Strawberry 
Statement." Here's a case where artists appear "courtesy of . .." as The Pink 
Floyd-Harvest Records, The Grateful Dead-Warner Bros., The Kaleidoscope- 
Epic, Patti Page-Mercury, etc. Those are some of the artists on "Zabriske 
Point." More up-to-date is the "Strawberry Statement" LP. Featured artists are 
Neil Young, Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young, Buffy Ste. Marie, Thunderclap New- 
man, The Red Mountain Jug Band, and some classical orchestras. Good albums. 
Another couple of commercial samplers are Columbia's "Heavy Heads" and 
newly -released "Heavy Hands" albums. Others include Capitol's ecology -geared 
package titled "Listen In Good Health," UA's "Progressive Heavies" album, and 
the "Easy Rider" hit soundtrack set on Dunhill. All these again include only the 
labels' artists or various performers from different companies. 
What I like most about the sampler and sampler -type albums is the very basic 
diversity of styles, voices, musicianship-all adding up to interesting, program- 
med blocks of music. One or two other labels have tried the Warner/Reprise 
approach to samplers, and several have tried the commercial scheme. The future 
lays bare to loads of possibilities of combinations of music and packaging in 
samplers. In the meantime, investigate refreshing yourself with a sampler. 
(Cont'd on page 40) 
HOLLYWOOD-THE CURSE OF THE AMOS HONDA 
Will Motown Records make the Bobby Darin announcement at the tenth an- 
niversary meet later this week? The label has been overturing to sign Darin 
for about seven years. Now we hear that he'll be cutting his first Motown LP 
in September.... 
For the past five years we've been referring (in print) to the Amos Tourna- 
ment as a combination golf meet and bacchanal. And each year our N.Y. re- 
write man switches "bacchanal" to innocuous phrases like "gala fest." Anytime 
that 70 guys get involved in an alcoholic orgy, we claim that's a unbridled bac- 
chanal. For those who don't know (including our re -writer) all contestants are 
required to "water down" (that is consume alcohol) at selected points dur- 
ing the two day meet. Otherwise they lose strokes. Minimum drink-every other 
hole-a jigger. That's old news for anyone who has staggered through the tour- 
nament or this column. But what has never been mentioned 
in print is the 
strange and terrifying tale of the curse of the $290,000 Honda. 
It started two years ago when Jimmy Bowen, proprietor of the Amos, decided 
to giveaway (as a rotating prize) his $220,000 Honda, a relic of his halcyon 
days as a hubby. When Bowen was granted his divorce, he claims it was at a 
cost of $220,000. "All 
I got was the Honda." In '69 Eddie Reeves won the cycle 
and the cycle continued. Within four months after the Amos meet in '69, Reeves 
was divorced-at a cost of $70,000. And this year the $290,000 Honda was 
passed along to Budd Dolinger, v.p. and g.m. of Mediarts Records. Budd was 
reluctant to accept the prize. We don't blame him. As of last week Dolinger's 
marriage was a cloudless affair, throned in highest bliss. But there's that omi- 
nous two wheeler parked in Dolinger's driveway on Wells Drive in Tarzana these 
days. So while Budd phones distribs to promote and sell his Orson Welles LP 
("The Begatting of the President") we wonder if he recollects the last line in 
the album-"come my brethren, let us pray." 
THE PRISONER'S SONG-We believe it was Mark Twain who said (or wrote) 
"what a good thing Adam had-when he said a thing, he knew nobody had 
said it before." In the record biz, like most other industries, originality is merely 
undetected plagiarism. A mousetrap by any other name is still a mousetrap. 
Still, there are a couple of albums in the planning stage that intrigue us. The 
first is a Sing Out LP that Dick Moreland, west coast manager of RCA's "rock" 
division, will be cutting at California's Tehachapi State Prison next week. The 
sides are due to be released in November. But most of the guys heard on the 
record won't be released for the next ten years. And though they have never 
recorded before, they all have records. Sides will feature 46 prisoners from the 
state institution, doing mostly spiritual songs-all original material with the 
possible exception of "Battle Hymn of the Republic." Songs were written by 
George "Sunny" Brown, former alto sax player with the Basie band. Brown is 
a three time loser, a great musician and an unlucky con. If memory serves, 
Sun Records had a quartet in the fifties known as the Prisonaires. But they 
cut singles only. The Moreland production will be titled "Tehachapi Sing Out" 
and Moreland says a college tour for the group is in the planning stage. That 
and perhaps a Hollywood Bowl concert. Dick also cuts Nilsson, Nesmith, Fat, 
Murray Roman and Rickie Lee, among others. Nilsson's next album, incidentally, 
will contain several selections from his forthcoming TV special, "The Point," 
and is set for Nov. release.

U. S. Vending Machine 
Shipments Down in '69 
CHICAGO - The shipment of mer- 
chandise vending machines by U. S. 
manufacturers in 1969 totaled $187,- 
515,000, down 9 per cent from $205,- 
126,000 in 1968, according to compila- 
tions by the U. S. Bureau of the Cen- 
sus which were announced today by 
NAMA. The 1969 total has been ex- 
ceeded only in three previous years. 
The number of machines reported 
shipped in the annual survey also 
was down to 505,076 from 564,121 
in 1968. As in 1968, reports were ob- 
tained from 36 vending machine man- 
ufacturers. 
The largest dollar amount was ac- 
counted for by beverage machines, 
with 1969 shipments totaling $119,- 
863,000, off 9 per cent from $131,- 
307,000 in 1968. Even canned bever- 
age venders, which had experienced 
spectacular increases in recent years, 
were down from 63,910 units to 61,- 
900 in 1969. 
The value of shipments of confec- 
tion and food vending machines de- 
clined 12 per cent to $41,149,000 from 
$46,530,000 in 1968. 
The only gains in the Bureau of 
the Census report were registered by 
post -mix cup soft drink machines 
(13,956 units vs. 13,760) and by hot 
canned food vending machines (5,134 
machines vs. 4,262 in 1968). 
"It's worth recalling that the value 
of merchandise, food and beverages 
vended through machines in 1969 in- 
creased by a record 10 per cent to 
$5.5 billion," said Dick Schreiber, 
NAMA 
president. "Although part 
of that increase represented higher 
taxes and prices, the sale of prod- 
ucts through vending machines is not 
necessarily related to machine pro- 
duction figures."

Betson's Sales and Service Blend Builds Ops' Confidence 
NORTH BERGEN, N. J. - "Service 
behind the sale," one of consumer 
advertising's more dubious claims, is 
deadly serious business in the coin 
equipment industry. 
For jukebox, 
games and vending machine distribu- 
tors, 
service 
support 
has 
often 
spelled the difference between consis- 
tent success and customer indiffer- 
ence. 
At Betson Enterprises, Inc., one of 
the East Coast's more prominent dis- 
tributing organizations, a close inte- 
gration between sales and service 
personnel 
has 
built 
up 
operator 
confidence 
and 
patronage 
to the 
point where the firm has consistently 
set higher sales records each year, 
even during normally slow periods 
which have hurt many of their fellow 
dealers across the land. 
"Confidence is probably the most 
descriptive word I could pick to de- 
scribe the relationship we have with 
our operators," Betson sales manager 
Jerry Gordon stated last week. "This 
means confidence in both the pro- 
ducts we sell and the people at Bet - 
son who sell them. 
"We live by a policy here which 
simply says: `never sell an operator a 
machine he doesn't need but if he 
needs one, make sure he buys it from 
us and back it with service advice and 
help.' Fortunately, we have top lines 
to offer. 
. Rock -Ola music and ven- 
ding, ChiCoin, Midway and other fine 
games lines, practically all the coin 
tables and the Automatic Products 
and Westinghouse lines. The product, 
however, is only half the battle. . 
the rest is to make sure the operator 
is satisfied with its performance on 
location and this is where service 
plays a key role. 
"First of all, people in our service 
Dept., which is headed by vice pres- 
ident Lou Avoglia, are thoroughly 
familiarized with the new machines 
as they are delivered from the facto- 
ries. If a customer has a problem 
with 
a new electronic amusement 
item, for example, chances are Lou or 
someone on his team can solve it 
over the phone. If not, we'll send a 
man out. You know, a lot of our 
customers 
have 
trouble 
finding 
qualified mechanics so we've helped 
fill that gap for them. Sure, some 
may abuse this and call for one of 
our guys for the slightest thing, but 
most respect our service people and 
won't request one unless it's really 
necessary."

ly sends people out to visit new ac- 
counts to give classes on the Auto-

EASTERN FLASHES 
THE BUM'S RUSH IS OVER AND THE GOLD RUSH IS ON!-With that charm- 
ing headline, we'd like to herald the passage of Labor Day, and with it, the 
return to bigger collections. Did a little digging around 42nd St. and learn from 
a couple of music, games, arcade and naturally peep show operators that trade's 
been down as much as 60% this summer. Times Square Vending's Harry Berger 
says the area has not been unlike a ghost town. "The area's so full of drifters, 
junkies and other riff raff, normal people are afraid to walk around here, and I 
mean during the daylight hours as well," Harry complained. "There's a movie 
out called 'The Out of Towners' starring Jack Lemon which pretty well tells the 
story of a couple of visitors to Fun City. They get mugged, cheated, robbed, you 
name it, and 
I tell you, if the Mayor doesn't clean the town up, the tourist busi- 
ness will be shot. Operators like myself depend upon a highly transient crowd 
in this area who visit the arcades, bars and the rest spend money in the ma- 
chines. We're losing all of them fast." 
UPSTATE ITEMS-Big John Bilotta says he's put about 85 amusement games 
into the New York State Fair, currently underway up in Syracuse. John's got his 
arcade in one of the exhibit buildings right on the midway and reports excellent 
business. Hot items with the crowd include ChiCoin's new Motorcycle game, 
three Gottlieb Batter Up pins (add -a -ball version of the Baseball) and Midway's 
Sea Devil target game. The Batter Ups, incidentally, are programmed for 2-250 
play, John says, and were shipped especially from the Gottlieb factory that way. 
Oh yes, Johnny's Rochester Lancers soccer team was slated to play Washington 
this past Saturday night for the Southern Div. championship; they've already 
won the Northern.

Number Eight 
Prod. Formed 
TEXAS-The Number Eight Produc- 
tion Company, whose purpose it will 
be to sign new acts and lease the 
tapes to major recording labels, was 
formed recently in Texas. 
Already completed for the newly 
formed company is an album by The 
Playboys Of Edinburg who were for- 
merly with Columbia Records. Little 
Women, a five girl self contained 
group, are currently completing their 
first LP, while The Family Lotus from 
New Mexico, is expected to sign with 
the company in the near future. 
Number Eight Productions has an 
affiliated publishing company with 
BMI which is known as Great Eight 
Music. All recording is being done at 
the Nicholls Studio in McAllen, Texas.
